#10038. NVIDIA Cosmos-H-Dreams: Bringing Real-Time Generative Simulation to Surgical Robotics

Surgical robotics is moving quickly from teleoperation toward increasingly capable vision-language-action policies. But evaluating and training these systems remains difficult. Physical robotic platforms are expensive to operate, experiments are slow to reproduce, and failures can damage instruments or biological material. Conventional simulators provide a safer alternative, but surgical scenes are exceptionally difficult to model: deformable tissue, fine instrument interactions, specular surfaces, sutures, needles, smoke, and occlusions all matter.

World foundation models offer a different path. Instead of manually authoring every object and physical interaction, they learn visual dynamics directly from synchronized video and robot kinematics. NVIDIA's Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator demonstrated this approach by generating future surgical video from an initial scene and a sequence of robot actions. It enabled faster-than-physical evaluation and synthetic data generation across the Open-H-Embodiment ecosystem.

Today, we are introducing the next step: Cosmos-H-Dreams, a real-time, action-conditioned generative simulator for surgical robotics. Cosmos-H-Dreams distills the capabilities of Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator into a causal, few-step student model and serves it through FlashDreams, NVIDIA's accelerated streaming-inference library. Running on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU, the result is an interactive environment that a person or a learned policy can control in a closed loop.

Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator is an action-conditioned world foundation model built on NVIDIA Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B and post-trained on the Open-H-Embodiment dataset. Given a surgical context frame and a future robot trajectory, it generates video showing the likely visual consequences of those actions. This makes it useful for offline policy evaluation and synthetic data generation. A recorded or policy-generated trajectory can be sent to the model, the corresponding rollout can be generated, and the result can be inspected or scored without repeatedly executing the motion on a physical robot.

Cosmos-H-Dreams moves the model into the real-time regime. Starting from the multi-embodiment surgical priors learned by Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator, we specialize the model for da Vinci Research Kit (dVRK) tabletop suturing and distill it into a causal student that generates the scene autoregressively. The released model receives an initial RGB frame and a live stream of robot kinematics, then produces the next chunk of frames before continuing with the following action block.

We have also demonstrated the versatility of Cosmos-H-Dreams by collaborating with CMR Surgical and Cambridge Consultants to integrate it with the Versius surgeon controller, enabling real-time operation on the Versius platform.

The key challenge is preserving useful surgical dynamics while reducing the cost of generation. Cosmos-H-Dreams uses a teacher-to-student training pipeline designed for long, autoregressive rollouts.

The bidirectional teacher begins from the Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator Open-H checkpoint, which uses a unified 44-dimensional action representation. For the released dVRK tabletop model, the dual-arm dVRK action content, consisting of relative end-effector translation, rotation, and gripper state, is mapped into this common representation.

The teacher is then fine-tuned on the JHU dVRK tabletop mixture, including successful demonstrations as well as failure and out-of-distribution episodes such as needle drops, missed throws, and unsuccessful knot ties. These failures are important: a simulator intended to evaluate policies must reproduce the consequences of poor actions, not only ideal demonstrations.

To improve stability during long rollouts, the training process progressively increases the teacher's temporal horizon. We start training on a 12-frame horizon and progressively increase this number until 72 frames. At each horizon bump, we initialize the warmed-up model with pretrained weights.

The teacher's denoising trajectories are first precomputed and cached. A causal student is initialized from the teacher and trained to imitate these cached trajectories. This warmup stage teaches the student to operate with causal attention and a streaming key/value cache before it begins learning from its own generated history.

Autoregressive models face a familiar problem: during training they may see clean, ground-truth context, while during deployment they must condition on their own imperfect outputs. Small errors can therefore compound over time.

Cosmos-H-Dreams addresses this mismatch with self-forcing distillation. During training, the student rolls forward using its own generated context. Distribution-matching supervision from the frozen teacher then guides those self-generated rollouts toward realistic surgical video. This prepares the student for the same conditions it will encounter during interactive inference.

The resulting model supports few-step diffusion, with as few as two denoising steps per latent frame, rather than the many-step process used by the full teacher. It combines the teacher's surgical priors with the causal structure needed for streaming.

Model distillation is only part of the real-time story. Cosmos-H-Dreams is served through FlashDreams, an accelerated inference library for autoregressive world and video models.

FlashDreams turns the distilled student into a low-latency streaming system through several complementary optimizations, such as streaming KV cache, CUDA Graph capturing, or model compilation.

Together, these techniques bring the distilled surgical world model fine-tune from the roughly ten-frames-per-second regime of standard Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator inference to interactive operation (~160 frames per second) on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000.

Cosmos-H-Dreams also provides the human-machine interfaces that turn generation into interaction. A browser client can send keyboard commands and receive generated frames over WebRTC. A Meta Quest client can map tracked controller motion into robot actions and display the synthesized scene through WebXR. The same model can also be connected to a learned surgical policy, with generated observations and predicted actions exchanged inside a closed loop.

While Cosmos-H-Dreams includes a pre-trained checkpoint for tabletop suturing, the system is designed to be extensible to your specific embodiment. To train a real-time student model for your own dataset, we provide a complete recipe for teacher fine-tuning and self-forcing distillation in our step-by-step guide.

Cosmos-H-Dreams opens a new frontier for surgical simulation: environments learned from real robot data that are responsive enough to be inhabited.

The immediate next step is to evaluate more than visual quality. A useful surgical simulator must respond correctly to actions, preserve instrument and scene structure over long rollouts, and support conclusions that transfer to the physical robot. This motivates a new family of closed-loop benchmarks: tool-tip reach and pose accuracy, gripper-cycle fidelity, idle stability, counterfactual action diversity, long-horizon drift, and agreement between simulated and real policy outcomes.

Real-time world models can also become active partners in surgical policy development. They can generate rare failures on demand, provide scalable environments for reinforcement or imitation learning, and enable rapid evaluation of new policies without tying every experiment to scarce robotic hardware.

Further ahead, real-time simulation enables a series of downstream applications such as latency-aware telesurgery, where the world model helps maintain a more stable display; or interactive surgical rehearsal, procedure planning, and intraoperative decision support. Cosmos-H-Dreams is a research and development platform, not a diagnostic system, a replacement for intraoperative imaging, or a controller for a physical surgical robot. Yet it provides a foundation for exploring these possibilities safely.

As model fidelity, temporal stability, and hardware efficiency continue to improve, real-time generative simulation can help connect surgeon education, synthetic data generation, policy training, and policy evaluation within one shared Physical AI environment.

Explore the models, data, and runtime behind Cosmos-H-Dreams:

Cosmos-H-Dreams brings action-conditioned surgical world modeling into the real-time loop, creating a new environment for people and policies to practice, explore, generate data, and evaluate what happens next.

This is a fascinating leap for surgical robotics. Real-time generative simulation could greatly reduce risks in training and planning. The concept of distilling a large model into a causal student model is clever. If you're also exploring video generation from images, check out the Seedance 2.5 image-to-video tool for creative applications.

Assessing more than just visual quality is the immediate next step. A practical surgical simulator must enable findings that translate to the real robot, maintain instrument and scene organization during extended rollouts, and react appropriately to actions. Tool-tip reach and pose accuracy, gripper-cycle fidelity, idle stability, counterfactual action variety, long-horizon drift, and agreement between simulated and actual policy outcomes are some of the new closed-loop benchmarks that are motivated by this.

The progress in surgical robotics is genuinely exciting! 🏥🤖 Being able to train and test advanced vision-language-action systems in realistic simulations without risking expensive equipment or delicate procedures could make development much faster and safer. The level of detail needed for tissues, instruments, smoke, and lighting really shows how challenging this field is. 👏

It’s impressive to see technology moving beyond simple teleoperation and towards smarter, more capable robotic assistance. 🚀 Better simulation environments can help researchers refine these systems before they ever reach an operating room, which is a win for both surgeons and patients. 😊📱

Looking forward to seeing how projects like NVIDIA Cosmos-H-Dreams shape the future of healthcare. 🌍💙 If these simulations continue becoming more realistic, they could play a huge role in improving surgical training, reducing costs, and ultimately delivering better patient outcomes. Amazing work and an exciting glimpse into what's ahead! 🙌✨

includes a pre-trained checkpoint for tabletop suturing

Chances are you’ve seen me on X: unpacking hundreds of MacBook Pros to deploy in a datacenter. The video hit a nerve: insane enough at the first sight, yet kind of rational if you know what we know now.

Unboxing Macs at scale for our new server racks.

So today I want to give some background into what it takes to build custom Mac racks, how we can start macOS instances from scratch in seconds and deliver new Xcode versions mere hours after Apple releases them.

Because our customers need Macs. And because Apple didn’t give us another option.

Many of our customers build and test iOS apps. You can't build iOS apps without a Mac. The iOS Simulator only runs on a Mac. Moreover, in order to release an app to the App Store, Apple requires using a recent Xcode version.xtoolxtool is cool, but it is not (yet) a serious replacement. So your coding agent needs a Mac.

But still, why laptops? Isn’t it a major waste of screen pixels and keyboard buttons and battery ions? Well yes, Mac Mini would be a better choice for a datacenter. Sure, it has very rudimentary remote management, no redundant power, and a beautiful case that ensures that cooling will be difficult regardless of which side you lay it on. But these are all known challenges that we have learned to manage.

But have you actually tried to order a couple hundred Minis? We have. Ordered in January, delivered in July. Welcome to the world of 2026 when the supply chains are in disarray. Never mind that Apple doesn’t release updated CPU models to all devices at once. So Mac Mini didn’t get M5 cores for 10 months (and then suddenly got M6 before any other device model!). We promise the best and the newest to our customers so we had to be inventive. That’s how the MacBook-in-Datacenter project was born.

Good design takes iterations; and we surely didn’t get everything right from the first try. But I think we have the system nailed down.

Every MacBook is connected to an IP KVM for remote management. Indispensable when dealing with laptops. Unlike Mac Mini, laptop firmware is designed with the screen in mind: some maintenance actions can only be done by clicking buttons in the beautiful GUI.

Of course, every MacBook gets an external 10G Ethernet NIC. Many folks at Namespace are networking geeks and we are proud of the connection speed and reliability that we provide to customers.

And then there is power. So in total, four cables per laptop, forty-eight per shelf, plus twelve for Ethernet, plus KVM wiring. Let’s just say that careful cable management is essential.

Heat management too. Currently we are deploying custom-made holders, designed to wick the heat from the hotspots and guide hot air away instead of blowing it at the nearby machines.

Naturally, we expected problems and challenges. Just not where they appeared.

I bet some of you looked at the pic above, saw MagSafe cables plugged in and already started writing a snarky tweet that MagSafe is not safe and may get accidentally disconnected.

And yes, I was worried about that too. But the reality is that we have seen very few cases of MagSafe disconnections.

The most unreliable cable? HDMI! Often thick and inflexible. Tends to fall out every time you touch the shelf.

Luckily by now we found almost perfect cables that bend exactly as we want them to bend. And we bought the entire supply of them. There are zero more of them available to order on Amazon.

Another source of pain: FileVault disk encryption. Or rather decryption. When a MacBook reboots (in an unplanned fashion) it prompts for a password to unlock the local disk. The prompt is shown on the screen (of a closed laptop somewhere in the rack, doh). No problem, we thought: we have the KVM connected just for this case!

Nope, not so easy. The password prompt disappears from the external screen after 5 minutes of inactivity. Then we remembered that macOS Tahoe introduced a useful feature: we could unlock FileVault remotely using SSH protocol. Still no luck. On laptops it expires after 5 minutes too. Looks like the only way out of this state is to reboot by physically pressing the button and racing to unlock in time.Mac rebootWhile on this topic, a small tip: you can reboot a Mac in a way that will keep the disk unlocked when you need it: fdesetup authrestart.

And then there are simply bugs. Under certain conditions, an external USB NIC stops working and acts as if it is not powered and shows no link. Trying another cable, another NIC, another switch port, no luck. But a quick visit to Network Preferences, deleting and recreating the “network service” in MacOS Settings brings it back to life.

At the moment we actually have it easy: M5 and M6 Mac Minis and Studios are coming into our fleet soon. They are way simpler to manage in the DC: they have a built-in 10 Gb network card, they boot up automatically after a power cycle and the OS can be configured entirely automatically via MDM.

But Namespace has some special sauce for the Minis too. We design custom-made shelves that hold the machines with focus on efficient cooling. We have tested a few designs using airflow simulation to arrive at what we are deploying now.

In the end installing Mac Minis is a breeze: unpack them, throw 10 pieces into the holder, connect power and network and press the power button once (famously inconveniently located). From there on automation takes care of them.

Under the hood a Namespace instance is backed by a virtual machine. We have multiple virtual machine engines integrated into a unified platform to run Linux, Windows, and Mac instances in the most efficient way. This way we can provide the same features that make Namespace special, like cache volumes, telemetry, or VPC connections.

Unsurprisingly, our Mac solution is based on Apple’s excellent Virtualization framework. It is an embeddable and flexible virtual machine engine. It’s easiest to compare it to Firecracker in how it fits the system architecture: it implements generic VM operations end-to-end as well as typical peripherals.

The Namespace VM host starts macOS guests through the Virtualization framework, which fits the system the way Firecracker does. Underneath is the Hypervisor framework, comparable to KVM. QEMU uses the Hypervisor framework too, but it can't run macOS.

For completeness, Apple also provides a lower-level Hypervisor framework, which is comparable to the KVM API of Linux. For instance QEMU uses it on macOS under the hood. Hypervisor provides a way to execute machine code in isolation, but requires the application developer to implement the bulk of machine architecture and peripherals. It could give us a lot of control, but unfortunately it cannot run macOS (it requires an Apple proprietary environment that third parties cannot, or shouldn’t, try to recreate).

In fact, most competing platforms are built on the same foundation. But the details matter: Apple gives us a few primitives that need to be arranged in just the right way to work fast and be secure. The more interesting thing is to watch how different people solve similar problems with different constraints.

A well-known limitation is that Apple only allows two macOS VMs per physical Mac. It can be a Mac Pro with 24 cores and 192 GB memory, yet it is limited to running only two guest VMs. This limitation leaks into our product offering: we can only slice Mac resources in two halves. So we run instances with 6 or 12 cores on 14-core Mac Minis and 8/16-core instances on 18-core MacBooks (we reserve a couple cores for management overhead).

Two cores stay with the Namespace VM host, and the rest split in half between the only two macOS VMs Apple allows per Mac. Each VM runs in its own VMM process, so hooking VM behavior or a custom virtual device costs an IPC roundtrip across the process boundary. On a 14-core Mac mini, the split is 2, 6 and 6.

An important consideration of Virtualization VMs is that the virtual CPU is executed by a separate OS process (VMM process in the diagram) from the software integrating Virtualization (here Namespace VM host). If we want to hook some VM behavior or implement custom virtual devices, every interaction with them requires an IPC roundtrip between the VM process and the “host” process. Such context switches are unavoidable and need to be taken into account when designing the system.

Virtualization framework offers a few ways to connect a virtual machine to the network. For instance, bridged and NAT networking modes route traffic directly from the VMM process to the host network interfaces. These are suitable for VMs running on a local computer where the workload is trusted.

Namespace instances run untrusted code and we need to enforce policies on what a VM can or cannot access (these policies can also be customer-defined!). Also we provide a few additional services to the instances that should appear “as if” they were on the local network for the guest system.

This requires us to take full control of guest networking in the mode where we process every packet that comes out and into the VM in software. We based our guest networking on a userspace TCP/IP stack from Google gVisor project and use it to implement an IP gateway/firewall for the instances. This way we minimize exposure of the host OS to unprocessed packets controlled by the guest.

Network packet handling needs to be very efficient, but as outlined above the path involves IPC. The VMM process needs first to pass the packets to the “VM host” process, which then processes and passes them to the network interface. It takes careful implementation and batch processing wherever possible to minimize the number of IPC roundtrips.

The above approach allows Namespace MacOS instances to reach 4 Gbps upstream bandwidth (per Fast.com). This is unfortunately still lower than the line rate. We have been exploring alternative approaches, including ideas on how to avoid IPC for network processing entirely. But productionizing the new setup is still left for the future. After all, 4 Gbps is still quite respectable.

Creating your first VM using Apple Virtualization is very easy: download a macOS IPSW restore image, use UTM/Tart/any of the dozens of open-source Virtualization wrappers to start a machine, click through Setup Assistant, install Xcode and you are good to go. Now you have a VM image that you can fork and run any workload locally.

But you need to test on multiple versions of iOS, so you install a few iOS runtimes. And then you install the upcoming Xcode beta version (and new runtimes too). And before you know it your VM image has grown to 500 GB (iOS runtime packages are huge).

You also want to have the previous version of macOS for testing that one little thing. Another 500 GB right here. Apple releases the new macOS developer preview, one more image.

And then you realize that the Xcode beta version subtly breaks the non-beta Xcodes on the same system (true story!). After all, Xcode installation bumps the “global” versions of CoreDevice and CoreSimulator. Hence any bugs in the beta Xcode simulator are visible when you’re using ostensibly stable Xcode versions. So now you are maintaining image versions with and without the pre-release Xcodes.

And now you have 2 TB of VM images. On what? A 2 TB MacBook hard drive?

That’s the challenge we faced: we need to build, distribute, and store huge images across the fleet of hundreds of machines.

Building images is a repeatable process so that we can reliably produce new images when Apple releases new software versions. Building is driven by a script that replicates installation and configuration as a human user would do it (e.g. the build script can run shell commands, click UI buttons or reboot the VM). Wherever possible we stick to using controls designed by Apple to configure the VMs in order to avoid surprising behaviours inconsistent with what a typical local user would be seeing. Naturally, building images is an automated and repeatable process. It is driven by a workflow expressed as a sequence of operations in a YAML file. Operations can be VM control (e.g. reboot), running a shell script or programmatic interaction with the system or setup UI over VNC.

Resulting VM images are handed over to Namespace internal Image Registry, in fact the same one that handles Linux and Windows image storage, replication and distribution (covered in the excellent article by Matteo). Disk images are of course quite different from normal container images: OCI layers are simple tarballs of files, while disks are generally flat arrays of bytes. Very large arrays in fact. And to a large extent they contain empty space: that’s the disk space that would be available to users as free space.

Naturally, it would be very wasteful to transfer and store the “empty” data in the registry. So we developed a simple format that allows us to preserve the “sparse-ness” of the images when stored in the registry. Unallocated spans of the image take just a few bytes.

And there is another important optimization. Remember the example scenario mentioned in the VM Images section: we have an image of the same system that differs only in addition of an extra Xcode installation. Obviously the latter image is built using the former as a base and most of the bytes are unchanged.

Our storage format preserves the “shallow copy” relationship and stores such images as multiple layers: the base layer is shared between them, while subsequent layers only contain the modified blocks.

Image A is stored as a base layer of block extents, and its holes take no space. Image B shares that base and stores only a delta: the blocks it changed and a hole where D used to be.

At this point we have the images in an OCI registry now. But of course Virtualization framework cannot start a VM directly using a disk residing in the registry. It needs to have something on the node itself: a VM disk can be backed by either an image file on the local host SSD, or it can route disk I/O requests to a server using Network Block Device (NBD) protocol. The latter would allow us to intelligently serve highly demanded data from a local cache, while conserving on-device space by not storing unneeded blocks.

But NBD has the same drawback as userspace networking from above: every I/O operation would incur an IPC roundtrip at minimum, including buffer copying and context switches. You see the same pattern as with networking: a very direct hardwired and fast option and an indirect “software-defined” but disappointingly slow option.

At Namespace we value performance a lot, so the choice is clear: we’ll serve the images from the local disk. We need to materialize them from OCI images in the registry on the SSD of every node in the fleet. 500 gig images to hundreds and thousands of nodes. And we need to do it fast.

Obviously, every node naively downloading from the central registry was not going to work. With the example numbers we are talking about half a petabyte of traffic transferred within, conservatively, tens of minutes. The registry (and the network fabric) would need to serve terabits per second!

The bytes that we are distributing are the same going to every node so the obvious solution is to organize a peer-to-peer delivery of these blobs. Each block only needs to be downloaded from the registry once by some node. Then another node that is close by (by certain metric) can download the block directly from the peer and we have two copies. So two more nodes can pull these bytes and so on. The fleet is exponentially flooded.BitTorrentObviously, BitTorrent was a heavy inspiration for this design. But unlike BitTorrent, which works in a public network of untrusted peers, we could make different tradeoffs leading to better efficiency and predictability. But that’s a topic for another post.

Each block is read from the registry once. Every node that has it passes it to another node, so the number of copies doubles each round.

Now the bytes are on the node disk. But remember the storage optimizations we did in the Build Process? With the naive approach of storing the images on disk there are a lot of bytes that are useless: they are either holes or could be shared with another image.

Some of you probably know that these are exactly the types of storage optimization techniques that are possible with modern file systems, namely APFS.ZFSLinux users have seen the same features in ZFS.

Using these cool features is also pretty easy: open a new file for writing, seek to offset 100G, write a block. And there you just made a file with a large hole in it. Only the block you wrote is allocated on disk, the rest is 100 GB of imaginary zeroes. When reading the file you won’t even notice the holes. The OS will return actual zeros.

Sharing the blocks is similarly transparent: just use the cp -c mode or clonefile syscall. The new file will share the same disk blocks and essentially not take any space.

hole.bin allocates only the blocks that were written. cp -c makes clone.bin share those blocks, and writing to the clone allocates only the blocks that change.

Writing to the cloned file is also transparent: as soon as you try to overwrite some blocks, these particular blocks will be allocated on the disk, while the shared portion will remain shared.

The pace at which we are expanding our fleet is increasing and the experience from all the above has transformed into a repeatable process. We know exactly how long it takes to bring a MacBook rack into prod. The rack assembly line is dialed in. DCOps people are trained. Disk images are built and distributed. We can bring whatever number of machines our customers need into the fleet when we need to (well, as long as we can purchase them at all).

We can still do better! What if there was a “holy-grail” device to host a shelf of MacBooks, providing power, ethernet and KVM connections over a single USB-C cable? It should be possible, yet there is currently no hardware on the open market that satisfies our requirements. So we are working on something very custom.

Or maybe we’ll do another crazy thing? What if we deploy phones to the datacenter? See what the future brings on our X soon!

InfoQ Homepage News Shopify Overexposed Scans GKE Ingresses and Cloud Run for Exposure

Nov 02, 2026 3 min read

Shopify has introduced Overexposed. This internal scanner locates Kubernetes Ingresses on GKE and Cloud Run services. It checks for those that are accessible from the internet without authentication. After a first version based on repository config files produced false alarms and blind spots, the team rebuilt it on GCP Cloud Asset Inventory and an anonymous HTTP probe. In just a few weeks of tuning, this reduced inconclusive Ingress verdicts by around 80%.

The original scanner checked the infrastructure repository for Ingresses. It focused on public hostnames without authentication settings and then probed them. Shopify says this failed in three ways. Teams that configured proxy authentication annotations directly triggered false positives. Admission controllers that rewrite settings at admission time, but do not run in every cluster, meant a correct-looking config could have no effect. Ingresses created by other repositories or platform tooling were never seen. The authors summarize the lesson as: the repository shows intent; the cluster shows what is enforced.

The current version follows a schedule. It queries Cloud Asset Inventory. This inventory includes Ingresses accepted by GKE after admission, along with Cloud Run services and load balancers. A second search retrieves access policies without needing cluster credentials. The inventory also surfaced Cloud Run services in projects the first scanner had never covered.

Each candidate then receives a single anonymous request. The scanner sends HEAD first, falls back to GET, follows at most three redirects and checks each one. It also tests path variations such as /ADMIN, since path rules can be case-sensitive. Results map to six verdicts: exposed, expected, protected, not found, unreachable and inconclusive. "Expected" applies when an endpoint is open but matches a reviewed, in-code allowlist entry by exact host and path. Allowlisted endpoints are still probed on every run, and an entry that turns out to be protected or gone is flagged as stale.

Shopify stresses that status codes are context-dependent. A 404 behind an Ingress means the proxy answered and the path is missing. On Cloud Run, Google's front end can return a 404 before the application runs, so the scanner classifies it as inconclusive. A 403 is also not treated as proof of protection. For Cloud Run, the scanner distinguishes ingress settings from IAM: a service is public only if allUsers holds the invoker role or the invoker check is disabled. Services behind a load balancer use a URL map. This map decides which backend handles each path. It also shows where authentication, like Identity-Aware Proxy, is required.

In early runs, roughly three in four results were inconclusive in one July run. The team grouped results by reason, added verdicts where evidence supported them, and replayed rule changes against saved scan results before shipping. Uncertain evidence stays inconclusive rather than defaulting to protected. The scanner stores verdicts, reasons and team ownership, but not response bodies or credentials.

Because the scanner makes outbound requests to arbitrary hostnames, Shopify hardened it against SSRF. It validates every IP returned by DNS, rejects private and loopback addresses, connects directly to the checked IP to prevent DNS rebinding, and repeats checks on each redirect. The authors recommend also restricting the scanner's network egress, including cloud metadata endpoints.

The team built Overexposed with AI coding agents and AI code review. To catch tests that pass while checking the wrong thing, they apply mutation testing to security guards and keep one canary target per verdict.

Shopify’s experience illustrates a split that applies to exposure scanning in general. Rule-based checks, such as Trend Micro’s Cloud Run rule, look for allUsers bindings. This is affordable and easily integrable into CI. This tool reports intent, not enforcement, so it miss resources created outside the repository and settings that an admission controller later rewrites.

Inventory-based approaches, such as Cartography and the Cloud Asset Inventory queries behind Shopify’s Overexposed, start from what the cloud actually runs, which closes those blind spots. Cartography still derives an exposed_internet flag from configuration, so it can’t confirm what an outsider sees. Overexposed adds an anonymous probe, an allowlist, and evidence-backed verdicts to the inventory. It sees uncertain evidence as inconclusive, not protected.

For teams creating something similar, use inventory as the main reference. Keep config analysis as an early signal in CI. Add a probe only if inventory can’t show whether access control works.

#10035. Windows pushed AI PCs, but now it's hit a wall of RAM prices

Customers sweating assets amid tight budgets, as Microsoft execs get creative with sales pitches

Microsoft wants enterprise customers to start thinking about PC refreshes using the same mindset – and line in the budget – as AI investments. The problem? Rising component costs caused by the proliferation of AI datacenters mean many clients are delaying client refreshes.

In a call to arms, Microsoft became the headline sponsor of the Canalys Forum in Barcelona early last month for the first time ever. Redmond needs distributors and resellers that convene at the event annually to get behind Copilot, Cowork and, more generally, AI computers.

Mark Linton, corporate veep for Windows and Device Sales, took to the stage to preach to a room he is hoping to convert.

"What we're seeing is the tokenomics of [AI] is getting very challenging," he said. "Having agents working on frontier models quickly becomes very expensive."

Redmond's proposed solution is to use those massive LLMs where most needed, "the right model for the right job," running smaller models locally at the edge on Windows PCs. "My goal, if we're successful in pivoting Windows to the agentic platform, is to have PC spend be part of the AI spend versus just PC refresh budget," he said.

"In an AI hybrid world, you'll be able to use edge devices, powerful PCs with lots of memory, lots of capability to run your AI workloads that are appropriate right there on the device. You keep the data locally. Of course, you don't have the token cost of the cloud. You have better latency, and you have more control."

Copilot is merely a component. This is not only about customers using Microsoft "first-party software" – it's for all models and all agents to use Windows as the platform, added Linton.

Goodness knows, Windows does need a shot in the arm. Microsoft last week reported profit and loss accounts for Q1 of its fiscal 2027, ended September 30, and revenue in the Windows OEM and Devices division shrank 22 percent from last year to $3.55 billion. Microsoft warned revenue generated in its Q2 may be down 30 percent.

"Growth will continue to be impacted by elevated inventory levels, PC market demand and a prior year comparable that benefited from Windows 10 end of support," Microsoft CFO Amy Hood said on an earnings call.

Market watcher IDC said calendar Q3 PC shipments sank to 62.7 million units, down 20.1 percent year-on-year, translating into 15.8 million fewer sales into distributors' warehouses. Tough macroeconomic conditions coupled with rising memory costs mean tough times for the PC industry.

Omdia – which owns Canalys – said: "The impact of upstream component cost increases has now fully worked its way through to end-market pricing, with consumers and IT decision-makers responding accordingly."

Reg readers know why component costs are going up. The datacenter construction frenzy meant memory chip makers could make more money from higher-margin HBM than conventional DRAM, prompting them to prioritize production of the former.

But AI PCs have been a tough sell from the start, as higher prices and a lack of killer applications meant many customers delayed purchases. Microsoft has to convince the market of the benefits – including trade customers as well as those in charge of procurement at enterprises.

Back at the Canalys Forum, Microsoft's Linton claimed customers mulling AI PC purchases want better productivity, to reduce costs, to innovate, and to be able to use these computers securely and at scale.

Microsoft is going to invest heavily in Windows from both the platform capability and security to enable these ends. So, if you are a Microsoft partner, you'll be able to run Windows and secure agents at the operating system level with Agent 365, with Intune, or with Entra.

Linton added: "We announced in June some of the technology in Windows, in particular Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC). And so essentially you can virtualize agents, and then you can use Intune to give them policy. And so other platforms, you have to manage agent by agent. Windows, you'll be able to do it policy-based, much like you manage people and network resources.

"You will have agents for all, and you need to know how to manage them, track them, audit them, and then ensure that they're contained in the right way. So we're doing that at the operating system primitive level."

Some of the quality control issues that have dogged Windows may give some sysadmins pause for thought about the grand claims made by the Windows exec.

Still, Microsoft is on a mission, and it knows how to attract thousands of resellers by dangling financial incentives in their direction. Linton said it is pumping money into channel programs, including AI-readiness funded headcount with "top partners" to "get this hybrid AI story moving."

Microsoft wants the channel to deploy AI internally too, "especially for your sales team" because "if they're using it, they're able to sell it."

Dell isn’t hopeful of an uplift in PC demand this year. David Kennedy, chief financial officer, said sales will remain "compressed."

"The reality is most enterprises this year for their IT budgets are sweating those assets out a little bit more and what dollars they have, they're trying to build out their infrastructure side," he told the Citi TMT conference in September.

"As we go forward, I think you'll see it [become] a little bit more robust. Our main focus will be on those higher ASP (average sales price) commercial boxes as part of the AI storyboard that's there."

He reckons there are more than 400 million PCs owned by customers that are "over four years old", and with the "cheapest token being closest to the data, none of those installed base PCs will have the battery life or the power to do AI workloads on them. So there is a pent-up demand that we believe will come once it stabilizes and once IT budgets get a little bit more settled and expanded."

Will 2027 be the year of the AI desktop? The Reg suspects not, though readers can do what they always do and speak their brains in the comments section.  ®

#10033. GPU Management: Why Idle GPUs Are the New Grounded Aircraft

Aviation learned this the hard way. For most of the industry's history, the number that best predicted whether an airline would survive was how much of the day each aircraft spent on the ground.

The reason is structural. An aircraft's costs accrue by the calendar hour: financing, depreciation, hull insurance, scheduled maintenance, crew contracts. Its revenue accrues only by the flight hour. Every hour spent on the ground shrinks the output side of that equation while the cost side keeps running exactly as before. Utilization also sits downstream of almost everything else an airline does. Turnaround discipline, network design, maintenance planning, crew rostering, and spare parts availability all eventually show up in that one number, because a broken operation underneath it keeps planes on the ground no matter what else goes right.

A bigger fleet still helps. More aircraft means more available capacity, plainly and simply. But two airlines flying comparable fleets on comparable routes can end up with very different economics, and most of that gap traces back to one measurement rather than fleet size.

Enterprise AI is running into the same structure, on a different piece of hardware. A GPU accrues cost by the calendar hour too, through financing, depreciation, power, and cooling, whether or not it's doing anything useful in a given moment. Its output only accrues by the compute hour. More GPUs helps in roughly the way a bigger fleet helps an airline: real capacity, a genuine advantage, and still no guarantee of the result that actually decides who wins. Two companies with comparable GPU budgets increasingly diverge based on how much of that hardware is doing something useful at any given moment, not on how much of it either one owns. That same number, like an airline's utilization rate, sits downstream of nearly every other infrastructure decision a company makes. Intelligence has carried the industry this far. Utilization is where the next real constraint is forming.

The scarcity didn't disappear as AI scaled. It moved up the chain, landing on a different resource entirely.

The first wave of enterprise AI was won on model quality. Bigger models, trained on more compute, evaluated against tougher benchmarks: parameter count and leaderboard position dominated the conversation, and the race produced models genuinely good enough to run real enterprise workloads. That capability arrives bundled with a dependency, though. Production AI runs on specialized hardware, and today that hardware is almost entirely GPUs.

GPUs are expensive, supply constrained, and in demand far beyond what's available, and this holds even at the very top of the market. In 2020, Microsoft built OpenAI a dedicated supercomputer: over 10,000 GPUs and 285,000 CPU cores, reported at the time as one of the five largest systems in the world, assembled to train what became GPT-3. At the time, it looked like an almost unimaginable concentration of hardware, the kind of number that made compute look like a solved problem for whoever could get access to it. Six years later, that number reads more like a starting point than a ceiling. By 2026, even the best capitalized labs on the planet were treating compute access as a live strategic constraint rather than a settled one. Anthropic alone was running simultaneous multi-gigawatt commitments across four separate hardware platforms, Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and AMD, layered within months of one another, while Meta signed a comparable multi-gigawatt deal of its own. Spreading commitments across four vendors at once is what compute scarcity looks like when a buyer has effectively unlimited capital and still can't get enough from any single source.

Six years apart, both events marked the frontier of what a lab needed just to stay competitive. What changed in between has less to do with AI getting more capable, and everything to do with capability no longer being the binding constraint.

The same pattern shows up downstream of the labs, in a different form. Enterprises consuming these models through an API run into a pricing problem more than a hardware one. Cost scales linearly with tokens used, and that single fact separates the economics of a proof of concept from the economics of production almost completely. A PoC processing a few thousand requests a month looks affordable. The same workload at production volume can turn into a cost line that never quite clears. The alternative gaining ground is straightforward enough: enterprises acquiring their own GPUs and running models locally, trading a variable, linearly scaling cost for a fixed capital one.

API cost rises with usage, while owned infrastructure stays close to fixed. Past the breakeven point, the trade reverses.

That shift turns the GPU into infrastructure rather than a line item, sized for growth, sized for demand peaks, and therefore sized above what any given week actually needs. Which means the purchase doesn't close the problem. It opens a new one. The day the cluster comes online, the question stops being can we get accelerators and becomes can we keep them busy, and only the first question had a procurement team assigned to it. Signing for the hardware is the part with a deadline and an owner. Keeping it off the ground is the part that quietly decides whether the deal was worth signing.

These deals describe capacity commitments, not efficiency. How well that capacity gets used is a separate question, owned by different people, measured far less rigorously, and considerably further from being solved.

A cluster full of busy GPUs can still be wasting most of its potential, and the reason is almost always the same one. GPUs run continuously, day and night, while the demand placed on them does not. Infrastructure has to be sized for the peak, the moment training runs, batch jobs, and real time traffic all land at once, which leaves a meaningful share of capacity provisioned and unused outside that peak. Better forecasting could solve that on its own if every GPU could absorb every kind of work equally well. Few can, and that turns out to be the harder half of the problem.

In the first generation of enterprise AI, a GPU's job was largely singular: run inference. Today the same hardware supports training, fine-tuning, quantization, real-time inference, batch inference, embedding generation, and model evaluation, often for the same organization, sometimes for the same model, on the same cluster. Each of these workloads wants something different from the hardware, and the differences run deep. Real-time inference needs low latency above nearly everything else, because a slow response counts as a failed one. Batch work cares about throughput and tolerates delay, sometimes for hours. Training can occupy a GPU continuously for a stretch measured in hours or days. Quantization needs a large amount of capacity, but only briefly. A scheduler tuned for one of these will misallocate the other three almost by default. The failure doesn't always show up on a utilization dashboard either. A cluster can report high average occupancy while several queued jobs wait for a GPU shape that happens to be busy running something else entirely.

The exact workload mix varies by organization. The shape of the problem does not. This is also where the aircraft analogy runs into its limit, and the limit teaches something rather than just qualifying the comparison. An idle aircraft can usually be redeployed to any route in the fleet: a 737 sitting in Chicago can fly to Denver instead of Dallas without much penalty. An idle GPU can only absorb a workload whose memory, latency, and duration profile it can actually serve. That difference makes orchestration harder than fleet scheduling, and it's why the question stops being whether GPUs are occupied and turns into which workload should run on which GPU, at what time, with what priority. Buying another rack of GPUs adds capacity and cost, not a fix for the mismatch, and that new capacity can sit in the wrong shape at the wrong moment just as easily as the capacity already installed.

Maximizing GPU ROI takes more than a one-time provisioning decision. It calls for continuous, active management of the infrastructure itself, running every hour rather than only at procurement time. What's emerging in response is a distinct discipline, GPU Management, an orchestration layer sitting between workloads, models, and hardware. Its job is to decide, continuously, which workload runs, when it runs, how it runs, and on which specific GPU in the cluster. None of this is exotic in concept. It's closer to what a good operations team already does by instinct, just formalized and running continuously instead of depending on someone noticing a problem.

Intelligence doesn't stop at the model boundary. The orchestration layer is making real-time allocation decisions the model itself has no visibility into.

Intelligence used to sit almost entirely in the model: bigger, better trained, more capable, and that was most of the game. Now it also has to sit in the infrastructure, in the layer deciding, moment to moment, which of several competing workloads gets the GPU that just freed up, and at what priority relative to everything else waiting in the queue. Keeping GPUs busy stops being the goal on its own, since busy is easy to fake by running low priority work that could have waited. Maximizing the return generated by each installed GPU becomes the actual target, and that turns out to be a far more continuous problem than the provisioning question that came before it.

Provisioning well doesn't make this go away so much as change its shape. A provisioning decision gets made once, at purchase time. An allocation decision gets made constantly: every time a job finishes, every new request that arrives, every shift in priority between a customer facing service and an internal training run. That frequency explains why the decision has moved from something a person handles case by case into something that has to run automatically. No engineer is watching a dashboard at three in the morning to decide whether a finished training run should hand its GPU to a queued batch job or hold it for an incoming burst of customer traffic. Something else has to make that call, continuously, and make it correctly often enough that nobody needs to check.

The discipline is new enough that its tooling and conventions are still forming, and no single playbook has emerged yet for what a mature GPU Management practice looks like. What has settled, at least, is where the constraint moved.

Specialization and orchestration solve different halves of the same problem.

Specialized, smaller models can perform specific tasks at a fraction of the resource cost a large generalist model would need for the same job, without giving up the quality the task requires. That has a direct effect on utilization. Workloads that once required a single, large model, occupying a large share of a cluster's capacity for the full duration of the job, can instead run on smaller, task-specific models occupying a fraction of that footprint. Capacity that used to be entirely spoken for is suddenly free.

How much capacity specialization frees varies by workload and model, but the freed capacity still has to go somewhere or it just sits there. A smaller specialized model only converts into GPU ROI if something is actively deciding what happens next with the space it frees up, reallocating it to another workload, another model, another queue waiting behind it. Left unmanaged, freed capacity becomes a different flavor of idle rather than a win, invisible in a different way than an obviously unused GPU, but no more productive.

Specialization without orchestration frees capacity nobody reclaims. Orchestration without specialization has less capacity worth reclaiming. Neither lever does the whole job alone.

Specialization without orchestration frees capacity that nobody reclaims. Orchestration without specialization has less capacity worth reclaiming in the first place, because the models are still large and the footprint they leave behind is small. Neither lever does the whole job alone; each one raises the ceiling on what the other lever can achieve. Neither is optional if the goal is to actually close the gap between installed capacity and useful output, rather than shifting where the waste happens to sit.

This is why model architecture and GPU management are two ways to address the same problem, approached from two different directions that end up leaning on each other. One shrinks what each workload needs. The other decides, continuously, where the difference goes.

A bigger fleet has always been a real advantage, and nothing here argues otherwise. Among airlines with comparable fleets, sometimes even a smaller one facing a larger rival, the winner was usually whichever one flew what it had more completely, carrying the weight of everything the airline did well underneath it. Enterprise AI is arriving at the same discipline from a different direction. GPUs are already installed, already depreciating, already committed. Specialized models and GPU Management are parallel solutions, or bivalent strategies. Specialization shrinks what each workload needs. Management maximizes the return on infrastructure. Enterprises that master both will set the pace of AI competition for the next decade.

The next frontier is managing an entire fleet of agents and there is nothing stopping it.

Agreed. And the part that isn't priced in yet: a fleet of agents makes per-token cost scale linearly with the business. At some point large enterprises stop paying that curve and bring the models in-house — which doesn't remove the cost, it just trades a vendor price list for a utilization number. And agent fleets are brutal on utilization: real-time inference under latency SLAs, batch jobs, retraining, evals — all bursty, all fighting over the same finite pool. Managing the fleet is going to be, in large part, a GPU scheduling problem.

Scheduling is the core bottleneck of this problem. A CPU-like isolation mechanism, or a sandbox-based architecture on GPUs, could significantly alleviate this issue.

Good point, isolation is a real part of the picture. CPU-style boundaries (and the GPU sandboxing now landing, like the Kata Containers work) are what make it safe to co-locate unrelated workloads on the same card without fault or memory-contention risk, which widens the set of placements a scheduler is even allowed to make.

Taking that a step further: once co-location is safe, we have to decide which workload runs on which GPU, at what time, at what priority, given that each one wants something different from the hardware (memory footprint, latency tolerance, duration). Isolation gives you a bigger, safer decision space; something still has to pick the right point in it. And rigid partitioning can even cut utilization, since an idle slice can't lend capacity to a busy neighbor.

That's exactly the direction we're taking next: an intelligent solution for job scheduling. We've got a follow-up article on it in the works, which will be published next week. Would be curious to get your read when it's out.

I expect we will see GPU rental systems become a thing. There are a lot of high-end GPUs sitting in consumer computers doing absolutely nothing for 90% of the day. Imagine if individuals could allow a training model to access their GPU remotely and in return pay them something in return. Yes, remote GPUs is not optimal, but with the consumer taking on the maintenance, power bill, and ownership of the GPU, any use the training model gets is a net positive.

#10032. Gist of Go: Concurrency

Many Go concurrency books and tutorials are like: here's goroutine, here's channel, here's select — use them as you like. Others just throw concurrent patterns at you without really explaining them.

This is not very helpful: the most important thing in concurrent programming is not pure knowledge, but the understanding and ability to apply concurrency primitives.

That's why I've created an interactive book that teaches Go concurrency from the ground up through practical exercises. These exercises are simple enough to be solved with a single page of code yet are closely aligned with real-world scenarios.

Audience and approach • Contents • About the author • Book details

The book is intended for programmers who are already familiar with Go, from language basics to interfaces and errors. You don't need any prior knowledge of goroutines and channels — we'll cover concurrency tools from the ground up.

Since the book targets experienced programmers, I've chosen a presentation style that I prefer: concise, focused, with exercises of moderate difficulty. Maybe you'll like it too.

Concurrent programming is a tricky beast, but I explain complex topics clearly, making them easier to understand. There are lots of examples and no dry theory.

There are dozens of interactive exercises that run directly in the browser. Each problem has an automated test suite that provides immediate feedback and a reference solution with an explanation.

There is no AI-generated or copied content. The book is 100% original.

#10030. Achieving nirvana: Enlightenment 0.28 hits the desktop

Very nearly 30something environment gets spruced up… and there's a new Trinity, too

Fresh on the desktop this week is a new version of Enlightenment as well the continuation of noughties hero KDE 3, the Trinity Desktop Environment, for those who prefer things a little old school.

Enlightenment version 0.28 is the latest release of one of the older Linux graphical environments, which first appeared in 1997. Version 0.28 arrives nearly two years after the previous release – we reported on Enlightement 0.27 in January 2025. If you're not familiar with this venerable window manager, often referred to as just E, we refer you back to that article, which also explains Enlightenment's slightly strange version numbering scheme.

Last time around we noted that its single-line release notes really didn't give us much to write about. The development team has made up for it this time, with some 68 lines of changes. It's both the same old E, and simultaneously a modern tool: it is still an X11 window manager, but it can also act as a Wayland compositor if you prefer. It offers conventional stacking resizable windows, but also can act as a tiling window manager if you prefer. On recent distros, it can now talk to the Pipewire audio server, and it can also work with NetworkManager to control network connections. This version delivers preliminary support for NetBSD too.

This isn't really a tool for newbies or those looking for a simple easy desktop. A sign of its age is that the first-run wizard asks if you want windows to activate as soon as you move the mouse pointer over them. This was traditional 20th century Unix behavior, and in the early days of Linux it was called "focus-follows-mouse," but it's rarely seen today. E isn't a full desktop environment: it only offers a few of its own optional tools, such as the Ecrire text editor, Ephoto picture viewer, Evisum task manager, and Rage video player. Even its taskbar is optional. It is more like a basis for experienced users to customize and build their own environment around.

The Trinity Desktop Environment has a rather lower learning curve: TDE is a port of the final version of KDE 3 to modern Linux. Proving old school is still cool, the project – which keeps the look and feel of 2005-era KDE 3.5 alive – has just announced TDE release 14.1.7, with dozens of bug fixes and plenty of new features. Among these is a tweak to the kicker/taskbar: you can now scroll the taskbar using the mouse wheel, flicking through your open applications.This release drops support for Ubuntu 24.10 "Oracular Oriole" but adds support for the latest 26.10 "Stonking Stingray."

Forks of older versions by users disenchanted with new versions are a recurring feature of the FOSS world, but they often tend to peter out after a while. TDE is one of the exceptions: we first reported on a new release in 2021 and again in 2023. ®

#10029. Introducing Adaptive Dark Mode

by Simon Fraser, Luming Yin, Lily Spiniolas, Joanne Pan, Veda Periwal and Jen Simmons

We’re excited to announce Adaptive Dark Mode in Safari 27.3 beta. When enabled by a user, Safari adapts light websites and presents them as dark.

In the spring of 2019, Safari 12.1 became the first browser to support dark mode on the web. A lot of people love using dark mode, but not every website has a dark version. Almost 40% of web page loads are from users in dark mode, and yet only 10% of page loads support it. If you love dark mode, you’ve probably hit a site that felt particularly bright. Adaptive Dark Mode is designed to close that gap, providing a consistent dark experience across the web.

You can try it today in Safari 27.3 beta. To enable, first make sure your system appearance is set to dark. Then browse to a website with a bright background. Safari will offer a preview of Adaptive Dark Mode. Tap ‘Try’.

For websites that signal support of dark mode with in HTML or color-scheme: light dark in CSS, Adaptive Dark Mode does not change a thing. For the rest of the web, it quickly analyzes the page, looking at colors and estimating whether it’s predominantly light or dark. If the page generally has a dark background with light text, nothing is changed. When a page has a light appearance, Adaptive Dark Mode adapts the page to be dark.

At the core of Adaptive Dark Mode is the transformation of color. Sometimes colors are simply decorative, while other times they have semantic meaning. Adaptive Dark Mode determines when to invert colors so elements remain visible or when to leave colors unchanged.

While creating Adaptive Dark Mode, we developed a color matrix to invert the luminosity of colors while preserving hue. It’s used to make light backgrounds dark, and dark text light. When transforming text color, Adaptive Dark Mode aims for sufficient contrast as defined by the WCAG 4.5:1 contrast ratio. Light CSS gradients are also transformed to dark.

Adaptive Dark Mode makes careful judgments so transformed content looks good and stays usable: buttons have contrast against backgrounds, text is visible over images, and hover menus look clear.

It takes the same care with images. Most are left unchanged, preserving their integrity. But many icons and logos can lose contrast when the background color behind them is inverted. So Adaptive Dark Mode inspects SVG images and transforms colors when needed. For bitmap images, it analyzes the pixel histograms and inverts simple black-and-white logos.

Effects like masks and mix-blend-mode can create undesirable results on an element whose colors have been transformed, so in some cases Adaptive Dark Mode turns such effects off. Also, content is left unchanged, since canvases contain a wide range of content that’s hard to predict.

In general, a web page will work well with Adaptive Dark Mode if it follows good modern web development practices.

If your site still uses older techniques, small updates can help. For logos and icons, swap bitmap images for SVG. Use solid or gradient colors in CSS instead of tiled background images. Replace image sprites with modern CSS for rounded corners, shadows, and button states. Create content images with transparent backgrounds instead of baking the page background color into the image. Add padding to containers to prevent crowding.

Perhaps you want a specific dark mode experience for a certain portion of the page. Apply color-scheme: light dark to the relevant element and add your own dark styles.

For complete control over how your site looks in dark mode, add full support. It’s a terrific time to do so. It’s never been easier.

All the web technology needed to fully support dark mode is widely available today, including:

Newer CSS functions like color-mix() and contrast-color(), plus popular techniques for organizing design systems with CSS variables provide additional options and flexibility.

Be sure to declare dark mode support using the color-scheme meta tag in your HTML head and/or by setting the color-scheme property on :root or body in your CSS. Don’t wait to inject this information later via JavaScript. This best practice helps ensure your site is rendered correctly as fast as possible.

If you would like your web app or website to not be transformed by Adaptive Dark Mode, you can communicate this using color-scheme. The HTML tag lets browsers know that 1) this page supports light mode and 2) should only be displayed in light mode. The color-scheme: light only rule does the same thing, but with the flexibility of CSS, allowing you to just target specific elements on the page — or of course, you can target the whole page with :root { }. (Note: the ‘only’ keyword is not supported in Safari 27.3 beta 1. Check back as Adaptive Dark Mode evolves through the beta process.)

As a result, Safari prevents websites from detecting when Adaptive Dark Mode has been applied. JavaScript that queries CSS colors will get the original authored colors, not the transformed ones. Any images drawn into canvas render in their original form.

If you manage a website or web app, and would like to discuss how Adaptive Dark Mode is adapting your project, feel free to reach out at web-evangelist@apple.com.

If you try out Adaptive Dark Mode as a user, and find a site that does not work well, we’d love for you to file a report with Feedback Assistant. (Learn more about filing Feedback).
