#9998. The cryptography behind electronic voting (and why paper ballots are still essential)

As millions of Americans vote in today’s U.S. midterms, most will use paper ballots, which are protected by strict chain-of-custody protocols and, in some cases, statistical audits. You may wonder why we still use paper for our elections and voting systems when tasks like banking, tax filing, and document signing have moved away from paper-based legacy systems and become fully electronic. The short answer: security.

That may come as a surprise to some. After all, cryptography and other security advancements have enabled secure electronic systems for many applications. In fact, cryptography can be used to provide two essential safeguards in elections: keeping (1) individual votes secret while (2) making the final tally independently verifiable. This is exactly the approach of cryptographic protocols like Helios and ElectionGuard. However, Helios intentionally targets lower-risk and lower-coercion settings rather than high-stakes public elections. ElectionGuard, by contrast, is intended for public elections, but not as a replacement for a paper-based system; it is used as a cryptographic layer integrated with traditional voting infrastructure.

In this blog post, we’ll explain how cryptographic techniques can help protect ballot secrecy and prevent manipulation in electronic voting systems, and explore the limitations of these systems. Although cryptography can strengthen election verifiability and have other strong security properties, it cannot fully replace the security and trust of existing paper ballot systems in general elections.

The National Academy of Sciences’ excellent 2018 report on election security concludes that electronic ballot return (also known as online voting or internet voting) should not be used in general elections, since “no known technology guarantees the secrecy, security, and verifiability of a marked ballot transmitted over the Internet.”

The difficulty of this problem makes sense when you consider the strong security guarantees any election system requires:

Ballot integrity must be maintained. This becomes especially challenging in the electronic setting because, in general, the voter does not hold a cryptographic identity and cannot sign their ballot cryptographically. Oh, and the electronic voting client and server may be compromised anyway.

Voters shouldn’t be able to vote more than once, but this is hard to verify without associating votes with their voters. This becomes even more challenging electronically when, again, voters often lack a digital cryptographic identity.

Everyone should be able to trust (and ideally verify) that the election result correctly reflects the voters’ intent.

Electronic systems introduce an existentially dangerous failure mode not present in modern, sensible paper-based systems: a supply-chain or 0-day vulnerability that can scale across many voting machines and jurisdictions could allow one person to single-handedly control and influence the outcome of an election (and, depending on the system and exact vulnerability, possibly while evading detection). In traditional paper-based systems, this risk is sharply constrained by independent physical records and physical security controls. It’s much more difficult for a single person to meaningfully change an election’s outcome while evading detection in this system.

Software security alone is not enough to secure electronic voting systems, though; the key design principle is not only to implement robust security controls but also to design your system so that all failures of those controls are detectable. This can’t be solved only using software whose correctness must be trusted. This property is known as software independence: changes in the election outcome caused by changes or errors (or vulnerabilities) in voting software must be detectable. In practice, this is typically achieved using evidence that can be verified independently of the voting software, such as a paper ballot audit trail.

One way of solving this problem is to threshold-share the keypair used for encryption, and split the private key between $N$ trusted election officials. This means that a predetermined quorum $t+1\ \leq N$ of the trustees have to be involved in order to decrypt ciphertexts. Using a homomorphic encryption scheme offers further protection for individual encrypted ballots: it allows the backend to compute an encrypted tally from the encrypted votes and only decrypt the final result. As long as $N-t$ election officials are honest, this protects the confidentiality of cast votes from the voting client to the inclusion in the final tally1.

With homomorphic encryption, the server can compute the encryption of the sum of the individual votes ${x}_{i}$ as the sum of the encrypted votes ${E}_{K}({x}_{i})$.

Schemes like Helios and ElectionGuard use a version of exponential ElGamal to encrypt individual choices on the ballot2. If the threshold-shared election key is $K\ =\ {g}^{k}$, the choice $x$ is encrypted as ${E}_{K}(x)\ =\ ({g}^{r},\ {K}^{r}{g}^{x})$, where $r$ is a random scalar. This scheme is additively homomorphic using pointwise multiplication of ciphertexts, as shown below.

Exponential ElGamal is additively homomorphic if we define $\oplus$ as pointwise multiplication of ciphertexts.

Note that decryption yields ${g}^{x}$ rather than $x$, which is typically hard to invert. However, since $x$ is comparatively small in this case, we can use brute force (or tables) to recover the exponent.

As an example, if we use 0 to indicate No and 1 to indicate Yes, we can compute the number of Yes-votes by summing the individual encrypted votes as described above, and then decrypting the encrypted tally to reveal the result. However, if we don’t ensure that individual ciphertexts are well-formed, a compromised client could simply encrypt the value 1,000,000 to vote Yes a million times. To prevent this, clients must include a zero-knowledge proof ensuring that the encrypted ballot contains a permitted value (or a permitted combination of values).

What if the voting client is hacked and alters the voters’ choices before they are encrypted, or drops the ballot completely? To protect against client compromise, the voter needs a way to ensure that the backend received their ballot, and that the choices recorded and encrypted by the software client correspond to how they actually voted.

This can be achieved in different ways. Helios and ElectionGuard use a mechanism known as Benaloh’s challenge method. The underlying idea is that when the ballot is encrypted, the voter obtains a commitment to the encrypted ballot and is then allowed to challenge and spoil their ballot. If they do, the ballot is opened and the voter can verify that their choices were recorded correctly and that the commitment corresponds to the encrypted ballot. The device has to reveal the commitment to the voter before learning whether or not the voter wants to challenge the encrypted ballot. Otherwise, it could present a correct commitment only when it is challenged. Moreover, it must be possible to obtain some external validation that the committed ciphertext actually encrypts the voter’s intended choices. Otherwise, the voting client can simply lie and present a plaintext that doesn’t match the commitment.

When the voter is satisfied that the voting client records their choices honestly, they record their choices one last time and cast their ballot, which is then published to a public bulletin board. The voter can use their commitment to check that their encrypted ballot is included in the published election record.

While this protocol provides a method to detect a compromised voting client that tampers with the voter’s choices or drops ballots, it still requires that a significant portion of voters exercise the mechanism in order to ensure that compromised clients are detected with high-enough probability3. Moreover, it does not protect against other types of compromise, like a voting client surreptitiously sending the voter’s plaintext ballot to a third-party server.

Additional issues must be solved in order for this method to be secure. One is the problem of voter authentication: how does the voting client ensure that the voter is eligible to vote, and how do we ensure that only one vote is cast? Additionally, there is the previously mentioned problem of coercion: how do we protect voters from being strong-armed into voting for a specific candidate or issue when voting stations may be spread out all over the world?

Authenticating voters is generally a difficult problem in countries (like the U.S.) that do not have a widely used national ID. However, there are options available for specific groups of voters. For example, some voting systems designed for overseas military voters use the Common Access Card to allow service members to identify themselves. Protecting voters against coercion typically requires that voters are able to vote without being supervised, which seems like a difficult problem to solve using cryptography.

If the election record is public (and we can ensure that everyone shares a consistent view of it), voters can verify that their encrypted vote is included in the record using their commitment to their encrypted ballot, as described above. This provides a mechanism to detect a compromised server which attempts to drop or alter votes. Again, we need to rely on active participation from many voters to ensure that a compromise is detected, since a voter can only detect if their individual ballot has been dropped or tampered with.

ElectionGuard extends this idea to allow voters to detect a change in any of the ballots cast before theirs by chaining ballot commitments generated on the same device. Without chaining, the commitment is essentially computed as a hash of the voter’s encrypted ballot. With chaining, ballot commitments are chained as follows:

When ballot commitments are computed as a chain, the hash chain is published together with the election record. Here, ${B}_{i}$ is voter $i$’s encrypted ballot.

This means that any changes are propagated forward, allowing voters to detect tampering with earlier votes cast using the same voting client.

Detecting a compromised server that injects additional votes is more difficult and usually requires external data, like voter participation records, to solve. It is not enough to associate encrypted ballots with voter identities, since a malicious server could pad the election record with ballots corresponding to abstaining voters.

Once the election record is trusted, it is possible to use zero-knowledge proofs to verify that the final result is computed correctly from the published election record. Since anyone can compute the encrypted tally from the election record, we only need to prove that the final aggregate ciphertext was decrypted correctly.

Recall our fourth requirement for election systems, which we admitted was most difficult to achieve for paper-based systems: Everyone should be able to trust (and ideally verify) that the election result correctly reflects the voters’ intent.

This requirement is usually formalized in terms of end-to-end verifiability, which means that the following should be possible:

Taken together, these two mechanisms allow voters to independently verify that their vote contributed to the election outcome, without relying on a particular piece of software or hardware (which may be hacked), or external observers (who may not be trustworthy). This property isn’t achievable in exclusively paper-based election systems without introducing some level of trust in humans/institutions overseeing the election. For example, without trusting anyone, how do you know what happens to your paper ballot after you and your vote both leave the voting location? The reason you won’t know this in an exclusively paper-based system is simple: in order to protect vote secrecy, when you submit your ballot to be counted with the other ballots, you intentionally break the link between your identity and your ballot.

Helios and ElectionGuard both build on the ideas outlined above, but their use cases differ. Helios explicitly targets settings with low coercion risk and advises against use in high-stakes public elections. ElectionGuard, on the other hand, is built to provide end-to-end verifiability on top of an existing paper-based voting system. Neither protocol makes a general claim to solve the problem of electronic voting because neither achieves the security of status quo paper-based systems purely electronically.

There is widespread agreement among experts on election security that paper ballots are essential for protecting the security and integrity of general elections, and that likely will not change anytime soon. However, cryptographic techniques like the ones described in this post can still be used alongside paper ballots to improve trust in the election outcome by improving the result’s public verifiability and auditability.

If you’re using cryptography to build a new voting system, please reach out. We want to hear about it!

A higher threshold is not always better. Helios requiring all trustees to participate to decrypt the election result caused the IACR to have to rerun their 2025 election after it found that one of the trustees had inadvertently lost their share of the key. ↩︎

Helios and ElectionGuard differ slightly in how they implement encryption. Here, we describe the method used in Helios since it’s closer to standard ElGamal. ↩︎

As an example, if a compromised voting client tampers with 1000 votes, and voters challenge one encrypted vote in one hundred on average, the probability of the attack remaining undetected would be 0.991000 ≈ 4.3 ∙10-5. However, it is also important to consider what recourse a voter has if tampering is detected. This determines whether they are apt to raise concerns, or simply shrug their shoulders and try again. ↩︎

#9997. As AI Risks Grow, Insurers Split on Covering the Damage

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

Some build specialized agentic AI coverage, while major carriers quietly exclude it — leaving enterprises exposed without their knowledge.

Following a rash of data breaches this year, several insurance companies have begun offering proactive policies related to artificial intelligence (AI) to cover enterprises that might be targets of unprovoked attacks or the source of attacks from AI agents going rogue. Meanwhile, other carriers are intentionally side-stepping this emerging risk, leaving enterprises to figure out how to manage it.

Insuring an enterprise against attacks from rogue AI agents that attack the enterprise, or perhaps those created within the enterprise that breach the corporate environment and attack third parties, is uncommon coverage. Many enterprises mistakenly believe their cyber and liability insurance policies covers AI-related risks.

As corporate insurance policies get ready to renew at the end of the calendar year, CFOs, general and outside counsels, CISOs, and other corporate executives tasked with insurance responsibilities should be examining them closely to determine their current AI risks and identifying exclusions that might be baked in. This is also a good time to meet with insurers that offer AI-specific policies to learn what types of coverage are available that the existing policy does not cover. Insurers are warning that the increased use of AI and AI agents is not keeping pace with enterprises’ governance. Rogue AI incidents, like the recent Open AI attacks against Hugging Face and other servers, have only heightened insurers’ concerns.

Related:9 Cyber Awareness Tips That Actually Match Today's Maze of Threats

Last year, insurance coverage specifically for AI-related losses was in its infancy. Carriers often included minimal coverage in generic Errors and Omissions (E&O) policies, Directors and Officers (D&O) liability insurance, or simply in the liability policy, but many of those policies are inadequate to address AI's actual risks.

Today, several specialty insurance firms have coverage for AI-related incidents, either as endorsements, language included in technology E&O policies, or as standalone policies. Among the insurance companies and specialty providers that sell purpose-built policies, affirmative endorsements, and specialized coverage targeting AI risks are Armilla, Coalition, Corgi Insurance, Cowbell, Munich Re, and Beazley.

However, several large carriers are restricting or excluding AI-related risks and autonomous machine behavior from commercial general liability policies, adopting the Verisk/ISO exclusion endorsements. The exclusions address gaps in policies that were written prior to generative AI becoming ubiquitous within enterprises, according to insurance industry trade publication Insurance Business. The ISO endorsement removes coverage for bodily injury, property damage, and personal and advertising injury arising from generative AI. Chubb, Travelers, Berkshire Hathaway, AIG, and W.R. Berkley are among those adopting this endorsement, according to the publiction.

Related:Rethinking Cybersecurity Awareness in the AI Era

So how can companies protect themselves from possible losses from potential risks from rogue AI agents? Here's what you can do today to reduce risk and improve your ability to qualify for AI-specific insurance:

Review your existing cyber and corporate liability insurance to determine which AI-related losses are covered and where your security exposures remain.

Analyze your network infrastructure to determine whether you have sufficient guardrails, along with specific policies and procedures, for addressing incoming and outgoing AI agent attacks.

Have your general or outside counsel review third-party contracts to ensure your supply chain is protecting you from potential AI threats.

Require your supply chain partners to demand their supply chain partners are protected; enterprises need protections multiple levels back down the supply chain.

Have your engineering team determine the different design patterns and architectural principles your vendors are using to build their AI applications. Not all AI development is compatible and responds to security software the same way; treating incompatible architectural principles the same could leave security gaps.

Be sure your AI applications have the minimum system rights and credentials required to do their jobs.

Treat Agentic AI as you would service accounts or endpoint detection and response systems. They're not "set them and forget them." They need to be monitored and maintained.

AI is not a panacea for every problem a company might face. It is a tool with specific use cases and configurations. If you use it as a catch-all for whatever ails your network, you will be compromised. Only use AI for specific tasks for which you have written rules, expectations, and results, and then ensure the AI applications are meeting those specific goals.

Related:Trust Is Not What It Seems — and Fraudsters Are Counting on It

Coverage for AI-based risks sometimes fall outside the purview of cyber insurance coverage. Because of AI's ubiquity in the enterprise, coverages for its potential failures likely will appear in other specialties as well.

For example, AI is used extensively by human resources departments in enterprises as a hiring tool, says Andrew Correll, head of underwriting for Armilla, a Lloyd's coverholder writing policies for the London syndicate. Coverage for AI tools that hallucinate or display a bias that triggers an insurable event might well be included in the enterprise's liability coverage or in coverage specific to use cases that are separate from a dedicated cyber insurance policy, he adds.

AI coverage addresses more than just a corporate computer being attacked and completely disabled, notes Craig Linton, AI and Emerging Risk Strategy Lead at Beazley. In some cases, a system only needs to be purged of unwanted data brought in by an AI agent. Taking systems offline for that purpose could interrupt business operations but is different than a common malware attack that forces the system to go offline or fail, which is a covered event. Beazley offers dedicated policies for defenses against the attack and endorsements that he calls "AI voluntary shutdown coverage," Linton says.

In order for enterprises to qualify for AI-related coverage, underwriters "look at the body of controls holistically," Correll says.

"Human review is obviously a component of that," he says. "But we also look for what kind of guardrails and rules are in place."

The Beazley application for AI coverage includes dozens of questions focusing on roughly 15 security controls, Linton notes. While most of the security controls are essential for cyber insurance coverage ­— multifactor authentication, backup and recovery, and training and network protection — the carrier also includes inquires about operational technology security, mergers and acquisitions, and Payment Card Industry (PCI) security.

He cautions teams buying AI insurance ­— often the general or outside counsel, chief financial officer and senior executives ­— that employees might be using unsupervised AI on their corporate and personal devices. Like similar shadow IT challenges companies faced in years past, employees will turn to shadow AI they can obtain easily and inexpensively if the tools are not provided by their employer and secured by the IT team. With AI, he says, this can introduce significant risks.

One challenge several sources mentioned is addressing the common problem of generative AI large language models (LLMs) hallucinating and displaying bias. For Corgi Insurance, coverage for hallucinated, inaccurate, or biased model outputs may fall under the Technology E&O policy/Generic Tech E&O policies written before generative AI technologies were widespread could be silent or ambiguous about how they treat model outputs. The company recommends looking for explicit AI-output language and reviewing algorithmic-bias exclusions carefully. When selecting an AI-centric policy, the proverbial devil is in the details, says Jack Kudale, co-founder and CEO of Cowbell. Does the policy wording address a nonmalicious system failure? Does it address an unauthorized disclosure without any external intrusion? Does that fall within a cyber coverage? Does it fall in a technology errors and omission, or does it in a completely different risk altogether? Questions like these will determine whether the policy or rider will address the threat the enterprise is trying to insure against or whether there is a possible exclusion, such as the Verisk/ISO exclusion endorsements and similar limitations employed by the top-tier insurers. If an exclusion is found in an existing policy during a corporate review, the enterprise then can purchase specialty coverage to mitigate that risk.

Protecting your enterprise from potential rogue AI agents and other AI risks requires that enterprises proactively ensure that three risk areas are protected: infrastructure, data pipelines, and your supply chain, Kudale says.

Protecting the infrastructure includes making sure that you have no misconfigured servers, overpermissioned identities, or exposed public endpoints. Safeguarding the data pipelines includes ensuring the storage architecture is secured from breaches, compromises, and poor decision-making, he adds. Finally, organizations need to secure their supply chain well beyond their direct vendors. Threats can come from secondary, tertiary, or further back in the supply chain.

"It's one thing we worry about the most," Kudale says. "We don't worry about hallucination and bias as much as others. We worry about supply chain more."

InfoQ Homepage News Google and Meta Open-Source TorchTPU to Bring Native PyTorch Support to Google TPUs

Nov 02, 2026 2 min read

TorchTPU is an open-source project developed by Google in collaboration with Meta that provides a native PyTorch backend for Google TPUs. It enables PyTorch workloads to execute on TPU hardware with minimal code modifications, supporting eager and compiled execution, distributed computing, and hardware-specific optimizations.

Google began enabling PyTorch workloads to run on TPUs in 2020 through PyTorch/XLA, which leveraged JAX, XLA, and lazy tensors. According to Google, this approach had significant shortcomings:

Crucially, PyTorch/XLA required intrusive source-code modifications to explicitly define compilable regions, suffered from severe compile-time latency, lacked support for PyTorch's native imperative (“eager”) execution mode, and lagged in supporting emerging distributed computing primitives within the PyTorch ecosystem.

TorchTPU takes a fundamentally different approach, making eager execution a top priority, and enabling existing PyTorch workloads to run out with minor code modifications.

Specifically, migrating from GPUs to TPUs involves replacing the cuda device with tpu and the nccl distributed backend with tpu_dist. Alternatively, developers can use the new torch.accelerator.current_accelerator API to identify the available accelerator, as shown in the following snippet.

TorchTPU support three eager execution modes: strict, debug, and DeferAndFuse. The latter is a new hybrid eager/compiled execution mode that Google claims "can be 50% or more faster than Strict Eager while reducing peak HBM memory".

To test TorchTPU's ability to run existing PyTorch models with no modifications, Google built an integration pipeline to evaluate about 5,000 Hugging Face models across 500+ architectures in both eager and compiled modes on TPU hardware generations starting from v5e.

We use a robust testing methodology grounded in corpus stratification and balanced architectural selection. Our approach relies on a two-tiered selection process designed to balance real-world adoption with broad architectural diversity, avoiding redundant testing of minor variations while ensuring real production weights are thoroughly evaluated.

To validate TorchTPU's performance, Google ran a 30-billion parameter Muse Glimmer model implemented in standard PyTorch. On a single TPUv7 chip, inference throughput reached 25.7k token/s at 5120 sequence length and 22.4k token/s at 10,240 sequence length. For training, using four TPUv7 chips, throughput reached 5.6k token/s and 4.6k token/s at 5120 and 10,240 sequence length, respectively.

Google also conducted experiments using Qwen3 MoE 235B for training workloads, scaling from 1,024 to 8,192 TPUv7 chips. For inference, Google reported competitive performance-per-dollar for large-scale MoE workloads using vLLM.

Commenting on the announcement, Hacker News user tingkuanpei observed:

Very interesting work. Google should have done this a long time ago. PyTorch's ecosystem is just so rich.

Other users pointed out that beyond offering TPUs through GCP, Google sells them to "enterprise client for on premises deployments", which include Anthropic and in Meta following potentially in the future.

TorchTPU is still at an early stage and therefore in continuous evolution. The project's roadmap include work on dynamic shapes, compilation performance, operator coverage, reinforcement learning, and quantization. For further details, make sure to read the original announcement, which provides a more comprehensive view of TorchTPU's architecture and scope.

#9994. Up to 3.2x Faster Inference with LFM2.5-DSpark

Today, we release DSpark draft model checkpoints for three models from our LFM2.5 family: LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct, LFM2.5-2.6B, and LFM2.5-8B-A1B. These add a speculative decoding path that trades a minimal memory increase for a large decoding speedup without changing output quality:

The decode phase in LLM inference is traditionally memory-bound. Most latency comes from streaming weights from DRAM into SRAM, not from intense computation. Speculative decoding addresses this by using a lightweight draft model to produce candidate tokens, then having the target model verify them all in a single forward pass, sharing the cost of loading the weights across all tokens we verify.

Over the years, multiple approaches of speculation have been proposed, with the most prominent being EAGLE-3, DFlash, and, most recently, DSpark, which combines three components:

We follow the DSpark recipe with a larger and more diverse data mix covering SFT, chat, code, and function-calling data. Based on our ablations, the first versions of the draft models are simplified attention-only draft models, with 5 layers and a block of 9. For each draft model, we ran 15 epochs on the entire dataset and selected the epoch with the highest acceptance rate rather than the lowest loss.

The resulting draft models are relatively small, with each around ~300M parameters.

Under greedy decoding, a draft token is only accepted if it matches the target model’s distribution. On rejection, the target model's own token takes its place. The emitted sequence is therefore identical to baseline greedy by construction, so benchmark accuracy (pass@1 or exact match) is unchanged.

Our DSpark draft models for LFM2.5 ship with day-one support for llama.cpp (implementation builds on top of the official codebase, which we run with experimental metal kernels) and **SGLang (**implementation builds on the official SGLang implementation of DSpark).

We measure on-device throughput with llama.cpp and Metal on an M4 Max MacBook Pro using FP16 GGUF weights and up to 256 output tokens. We measure GPU throughput with SGLang on a single H100 80 GB in BF16. Both configurations use a DSpark block size of 9, a batch size of 1, and a temperature of 0. We evaluate them on five benchmark datasets.

All three drafter models deliver noticeable throughput improvements on both the large-scale accelerator (H100) and the edge deployment (M4 Max MacBook).

For LFM2.5-2.6B, speedup on the MacBook is especially noticeable, as it pushes the interactivity level a user can enjoy far beyond the throughput offered by most proprietary cloud models (around ~140 tok/s, depending on the dataset).

Across various multi-tool scenarios, DSpark reduces the latency by 57% on average for LFM2.5-2.6B.

For LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct, we see much more variance in dataset acceptance rates, so speedup varies by as much as 52% depending on the underlying text distribution.

For LFM2.5-8B-A1B, the acceptance rate increases compared to two dense models, yet on-device we get only an 18% improvement on average. This gap is due to the current MoE implementation in llama.cpp's Metal backend, and to the fact that verifying k tokens activates more experts and thus more weight traffic than a single decode step.

Running the DSpark draft models with SGLang requires an SGLang build with DSpark support for LFM2 targets (PR #31041). Launch the target with the draft attached:

Then query the OpenAI-compatible endpoint at http://localhost:30000/v1. The block size is read from the draft's config.json; the baseline is the same command without the three --speculative-* flags.

Running them with llama.cpp requires the respective llama.cpp build (PR#27383).

The block size is read from the sidecar metadata (n-max is clamped to it). Speculative decoding is exact: the target verifies every proposed token, so greedy output equals the target alone; per-response timings report draft_n / draft_n_accepted.

The DSpark draft model checkpoints are available on Hugging Face as Safetensors and in GGUF format:

For citations, please use the following reference or BibTeX:

Liquid AI, "LFM2.5-DSpark: Up to 3.2x Faster Inference from H100 to MacBook", Liquid AI Blog, Aug 2026.

#9993. Les supermarchés de l'UE paient d'un firmware de réfrigérateur non mis à jour

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Des centaines de magasins ont subi des pertes se chiffrant en millions d'euros parce qu'ils avaient fait appel à des tiers pour gérer le micrologiciel OT obsolète qui pilotait leurs systèmes de climatisation.

This translation is provided by our internal AI translation tool.

Des centaines de supermarchés français ont subi cette semaine des pertes s'élevant à plusieurs dizaines, voire plusieurs centaines de millions d'euros, à la suite de cyberattaques qui ont perturbé leurs systèmes de réfrigération.

Dans la nuit de lundi, des pirates informatiques ont piraté les contrôleurs des systèmes de réfrigération commerciaux de grandes chaînes de supermarchés françaises. Ils ont transformé les réfrigérateurs, les congélateurs et les chambres froides en appareils de chauffage, faisant grimper leur température jusqu’à 50 degrés Celsius (plus de 120 degrés Fahrenheit), ce qui a complètement abîmé tous les aliments qu’ils contenaient et aurait même provoqué quelques petits incendies. L’identité et les motivations de l’auteur de cette attaque restent inconnues.

Les contrôleurs de réfrigération permettent aux commerçants de régler et de surveiller à distance la température de leurs réfrigérateurs, 24 heures sur 24 et 7 jours sur 7. Il s’ensuit donc que les gérants de magasin auraient pu être alertés ou se rendre compte manuellement que quelque chose n’allait pas. Pour empêcher cela, des sources françaises indiquent que les attaquants ont prolongé les cycles de dégivrage des systèmes ciblés — processus au cours duquel les congélateurs font fondre intentionnellement le givre et la glace accumulés — afin que le réchauffement passe pour un entretien de routine.

Related:EU Grocers Pay a Steep Price for Unpatched Fridge Firmware

Selon les propres rapports des entreprises, les attaques ont touché un peu plus de 700 magasins d’alimentation et commerces de détail, tous au cours de la même nuit. Un analyste de la société française de cybersécurité Sekoia a déclaré à Reuters que l’Espagne, le Portugal, la Pologne, l’Allemagne et la Belgique avaient également été touchés, et qu’une grande chaîne de supermarchés aux Pays-Bas avait mis ses systèmes hors service par mesure de précaution, selon l’AP. Une seule chaîne française, Intermarché, a fait état de pertes s’élevant à plusieurs dizaines de millions d’euros.

Pire encore, les experts soulignent que ces attaques auraient très certainement pu être évitéesgrâce à des mesures élémentaires de cybersécurité.

Les premiers rapports suggéraient que les attaques de lundi étaient liées aux contrôleurs de réfrigération du fabricant danois Danfoss. Danfoss occupe une place importante dans le domaine des solutions de contrôle pour les supermarchés et la grande distribution alimentaire, avec plus de 50 000 installations de sa technologie à travers le monde, selon son site web.

Related:Taiwan Bullet Train Hack Highlights Cybersecurity Gaps in Rail Systems

Le 9 août, des chercheurs en cybersécurité de l’équipe Team82 de Claroty ont révélé trois vulnérabilités dans la plateforme AK-SM 800A de Danfoss. Ces failles — référencées sous les numéros CVE-2025-41450, CVE-2025-41451 et CVE-2025-41452 — permettaient aux attaquants de procéder à l’exécution de code à distance (RCE) ou à un déni de service (DoS) contre les parcs de réfrigération des entreprises. Danfoss a corrigé ces failles mais comptait sur ses clients pour mettre à jour eux-mêmes leurs systèmes.

Dans une déclaration à Reuters, Danfoss a rejeté la responsabilité sur les clients utilisant un micrologiciel obsolète, indiquant qu’elle « conseillait depuis longtemps à ses clients de maintenir les systèmes pris en charge à jour avec le dernier micrologiciel et de migrer les systèmes hérités vers des solutions de dernière génération ».Le fabricant d'équipement d'origine (OEM) a fourni davantage d'informations à une publication spécialisée dans la réfrigération, Cooling Post. Selon lui, la « majorité » des unités concernées fonctionnaient sous AK-SM 800 ou son prédécesseur, l'AK-SC355. Ces deux systèmes ont depuis longtemps atteint leur fin de vie : le premier en 2021, le second en 2016.

Related:AI-Driven Cyberattack on Mexico Couldn't Breach OT Systems

Mardi, le CERT national français (CERT-FR) avait identifié qu’une autre plateforme de contrôleurs de réfrigération — « XWEB », des fournisseurs Dixell et de sa société mère Copeland — avait également été impliquée dans les attaques. Il n’a pas précisé quelles vulnérabilités ou versions de micrologiciel pouvaient être en cause, bien que les indices circonstanciels indiquent désormais clairement que les auteurs de ces menaces s’appuient sur les recherches de Team82. Le jour même où ils ont révélé ces vulnérabilités affectant Danfoss, ces mêmes chercheurs ont divulgué 23 autres touchant XWEB Pro, dont 21 de gravité élevée.

Le 26 août, une série étrange de rapports similaires a commencé à filtrer depuis des installations militaires américaines.Les groupes frigorifiques tombaient en panne. Dans chaque base où cela se produisait, les gens ont probablement pensé qu’il s’agissait d’un problème électrique inhabituel. Mais peu à peu, de plus en plus de sites ont signalé le même phénomène.

Après être tombée sur ces rapports étranges sur les réseaux sociaux, une journaliste indépendante a émis une hypothèse hasardeuse. « Je suis suffisamment lucide pour savoir que cela semble insensé, mais je vous demande de me suivre », a écrit M. Elizabeth sur Substack. « Je pense qu’il y a une probabilité non nulle que quelqu’un ait piraté les congélateurs des commissariats. »

À ce jour, l’armée américaine n’a pas confirmé qui ou quoi était à l’origine des pannes survenues dans les cantines réparties sur au moins 14 bases de l’armée de l’air, installations de la marine et postes de l’armée de terre distincts. Il se pourrait que ce soit une coïncidence que ces attaques aient eu lieu seulement deux semaines après la divulgation des vulnérabilités par Danfoss.

Ce serait d’autant plus une coïncidence que la Defense Commissary Agency (DeCA) — l’agence centrale du ministère de la Défense (DoD) chargée de superviser les magasins militaires — a explicitement mentionné avoir utilisé les technologies de Danfoss par le passé. Par exemple, dans un modèle de cahier des charges techniquedestiné aux prestataires des magasins militaires datant de juin 2022, la DeCA citait le Danfoss AK-SM 800A comme « base de conception » pour les différentes unités de contrôle.

Fort de son expérience, Bill Moore, PDG de Xona Systems, se souvient : « Dans bon nombre de ces magasins physiques — mais aussi dans les usines de fabrication, les centrales électriques, les sites pétroliers et gaziers, c’est le cas partout —, le plus gros problème est que les organisations parviennent plutôt bien à segmenter leurs propres réseaux. Mais en matière de technologies opérationnelles (OT), il y a tous ces équipementiers et tiers qui ont besoin d’un accès. Et les entreprises n’y ont pas vraiment prêté attention. »

En accordant à de nombreux fournisseurs et équipementiers l’accès à leurs systèmes, les entreprises finissent par s’exposer à des attaques à distance. « Et il n’y a littéralement aucune visibilité ni gouvernance sur bon nombre de ces connexions. Je dirais que c’est vrai dans un pourcentage élevé de cas — la moitié, peut-être plus, dans l’ensemble. Elles laissent en quelque sorte tous leurs équipementiers agir à leur guise, mais nous avons constaté que de nombreux pirates compromettent ces connexions tierces », déplore-t-il.

Dans un e-mail adressé à CNBC, Les Mousquetaires — société mère d’Intermarché et de Netto — a expliqué que l’attaque avait eu lieu via un prestataire de services chargé des systèmes de réfrigération dans certains de ses magasins.

« En résumé : déconnectez vos équipements d’Internet », déclare Andrew Ginter, vice-président chargé de la sécurité industrielle chez Waterfall Security Solutions. Les recherches effectuées cette semaine sur Shodan ont par exemple révélé des milliers de systèmes Danfoss exposés sur Internet, dont environ 1 500 rien qu’en France.

« Dans un monde idéal, les entreprises protégeraient leurs systèmes de contrôle derrière un accès à distance contrôlé par du matériel », explique M. Ginter, « mais même un simple pare-feu entre ces appareils et Internet serait déjà utile. »

Pour les pare-feu de base, il conseille aux entreprises :

De mettre en place une règle « tout refuser »

De n’autoriser les connexions qu’à partir d’adresses IP spécifiques

D’appliquer un mot de passe et une authentification à deux facteurs à ces connexion

De mettre à jour automatiquement le pare-feu, pour éviter de l’oublier

Utilisent des appareils de qualité commerciale ou industrielle, et non grand public ; de nombreux appareils grand public ne proposent pas de mises à jour, ou ne se mettent pas à jour rapidement

Enfin, ajoute-t-il, « Remplacez le pare-feu strictement tous les quatre ans. Pourquoi ? Parce que si nous avons des appareils exposés à Internet, neuf fois sur dix, nous n’avons pas d’équipe de sécurité, et nous ne remarquerons pas quand nos pare-feu ne seront plus pris en charge et que les mises à jour automatiques cesseront. »

« Les mesures de base ne suffisent pas pour les infrastructures critiques de grande envergure ou l’industrie lourde, mais elles contribueront grandement à empêcher les hacktivistes de s’introduire dans vos congélateurs », conclut Ginter. « Retirez vos équipements d’Internet. Faites-le de toute urgence. »

Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

#9992. How We Could Have Backdoored Bash (Hacktron blog)

Given the increase in supply chain attacks, I really don't understand why so many projects still feel comfortable to fully rely on centralized, server-side security mechanisms. Almost every time I look at a real or potential supply chain attack, I cannot help but wonder how much more difficult or fragile the attack would have been if regular code signing would be more ubiquitous.

Almost every modern system has a HSM, Secure Enclave, or whatever; and if you don't like those, there are OpenPGP-smartcards, YubiKeys, ... you name it. If you don't like PGP, OpenSSH also supports signing for over six years now, including FIDO2-backed signatures. Git support for OpenPGP signatures goes back for decades, and OpenSSH signatures are also supported for more than 5 years now. Yet, nobody seems to care – worse, even basic infrastructure like cargo, pip, npm, etc., don't offer an optional possibility to attach and require signatures.

To be clear: I neither blame individual developers nor maintainers; I'm a big fan of provided-as-is – nobody should be forced to buy a YubiKey just because they are hobby devs. Nonetheless if we operate at an institutional scale, where we have legal entities and supply core infrastructure... I don't get it – not even to blame someone, I just simply don't get it.

Classical banking provides a more nuanced (if less formalized) picture. Entities have credit risk, collateral must be made available, and all sorts of derivatives are traded against those things. The trading is both hedging (to protect yourself against a business partner's default) and speculative (because you have an opinion about their decline or recovery). Clearing houses like the Options Clearing Corporation create a safe harbor for mutual trust by holding its members to a high standard of credit-worthiness. In technology we have lots of perfectly correct, cryptographically-sound signing solutions. We don't have the semi-formal credit systems that banking has shown to mostly work. I think this is largely because trust is radically efficient, and mistrust carries a lot of overhead and capital drag. It's better if we can rely on trust, but best if we could formalize credit efficiently and solve for distributed trust management.

In technology we have lots of perfectly correct, cryptographically-sound signing solutions. We don't have the semi-formal credit systems that banking has shown to mostly work. I think this is largely because trust is radically efficient, and mistrust carries a lot of overhead and capital drag. It's better if we can rely on trust, but best if we could formalize credit efficiently and solve for distributed trust management.

Even if you have full cryptographic signing, there are still classes of attacks that compromise the keys or certificates and break it open.

Definitely, trust is hard, and code signing is by no means a silver bullet; it only helps against certain attack scenarios, and also has to be applied correctly. Nonetheless, E2E signature chains make a lot of attacks much harder or fragile or – in abstract terms – more expensive.

It's a bit like saying: TLS is not perfect, CAs are not secure, and someone might roll a private key of 4 (obligatory xkcd). Nonetheless, nobody would seriously argue that we probably should ditch TLS and go back to plain HTTP.

Of course, this doesn't scale well (especially to regular people which often don't even know what TLS is), but if you don't need to trust many web servers (and I don't) and your users are capable of verifying a PGP signature manually (mine can), it can be enough.

I might be wrong there, but I had the impression that if the user chooses to import your site's certificate system-wide the only option they have for that is to make it a trust anchor, and therefore allow it to act as a CA, because (from my understanding) quite a few TLS clients assume that all trust anchors are inherently allowed to act as CAs, and cert extensions like basicConstraints (which says "this is an end entity and not a CA") are only honored at least one level down from that. So if I've got that right, then making your users treat each web or TLS server as a potential CA exposes them to more risk (as each server has its key online) compared to having a real personal CA (whose key you can guard properly). This is on top of needing to repeat the PGP verification step manually for each new server (or each new key rotation), rather than verifying the private CA just once... (And of course trust anchors can't be revoked except for everyone removing them manually, whereas if your one server's key is compromised, your private CA can issue a CRL – which most of Linux TLS ecosystem sadly doesn't check, lagging 30 years behind other platforms, but at least I think the major web browsers do.)

Hmmm, I don't know. I set `basicConstraints = CA:FALSE`, but if clients ignore that, then I'd say it's a bug in clients. > So if I've got that right, then making your users treat each web or TLS server as a potential CA exposes them to more risk (as each server has its key online) compared to having a real personal CA (whose key you can guard properly). > > This is on top of needing to repeat the PGP verification step manually for each new server (or each new key rotation), rather than verifying the private CA just once... I've been considering that option. I'm not experienced enough in OpenSSL to have a CA myself, but I'd consider eventually having one. Of course, I'd like to restrict it to emitting certificates for my domains only, and I'd sign the CA itself with my PGP key, but indeed, it would be an improvement over what I'm doing now. > trust anchors can't be revoked That's not a big deal. I assume and ask users to assume that my server is not trusted, and that the only things they can trust from it are the PGP-signed commits in the git repositories. The reason I provide TLS is not for authenticating my server (I don't consider it authentic myself), but rather for encrypting (at least part of) the requests and responses, so that people sniffing (and perhaps injecting adds or other stuff) have it at least more difficult.

That's not a big deal. I assume and ask users to assume that my server is not trusted, and that the only things they can trust from it are the PGP-signed commits in the git repositories. The reason I provide TLS is not for authenticating my server (I don't consider it authentic myself), but rather for encrypting (at least part of) the requests and responses, so that people sniffing (and perhaps injecting adds or other stuff) have it at least more difficult.

For v3 certificates CA:FALSE is also the default if the whole extension is absent. The point though is that trust anchors have different treatment from regular certificates. I've heard that some platforms ignore most of the metadata of a cert that's been specified as a trust anchor (e.g. root CA expiry dates certainly seem to be commonly ignored), and/or the fact that they're installed into a "Trusted *authorities*" store is interpreted as a user override of the CA:FALSE, and/or something along those lines. So if one tells users "install my web server's self-signed certificate into /etc/ssl/certs, it has CA:FALSE so it's safe", I'd be more than a little cautious about that. Well, of course, the same goes for a whole personal CA – but what I mean to say is, telling users "install my whole CA into /etc/ssl/certs" is *explicitly* an informed trust decision, while telling users "install my web server cert into /etc/ssl/certs" can be an accidental trust decision that *looks* like it is scoped to a single server but secretly is much broader. Yes, I too would love the ability to install TLS CAs that are scoped to a single domain subtree (like how it is possible with OpenSSH's certificates), or at least wider support of 'nameConstraints' (the extension that truly restricts a CA to only your domain and which half the things happily ignore). But unfortunately we're not even at the point yet where most Linux software could distinguish basic trust purposes - only Mozilla's NSS has distinct "trusted for TLS" and "trusted for S/MIME", and p11-kit has been *trying* to expose that to the broader ecosystem, but most software is still at the caveman level of "everything in ca-certificates.pem is trusted permanently for every purpose"... > I've been considering that option. I'm not experienced enough in OpenSSL to have a CA myself, but I'd consider eventually having one. Of course, I'd like to restrict it to emitting certificates for my domains only, and I'd sign the CA itself with my PGP key, but indeed, it would be an improvement over what I'm doing now. Honestly OpenSSL's own tooling isn't great, it has an "openssl ca" but its usability is, ehh. The "easy-rsa" script that comes with OpenVPN might be an improvement. For a GUI, the Qt-based XCA seemed alright as well. (Smallstep (step-ca) also seems relatively popular but it is Infrastructure, not a standalone tool. It didn't quite click for me; I ended up writing my own CA in Ruby's openssl libraries, then another using python-certbuilder, then another using python-cryptography...) > The reason I provide TLS is not for authenticating my server (I don't consider it authentic myself), but rather for encrypting (at least part of) the requests and responses, so that people sniffing (and perhaps injecting adds or other stuff) have it at least more difficult. I think those are rather intertwined. On the one hand, if all you want is encryption, you don't even need the "PGP verification" part at all, just throw together any dummy certificate and it'll do the job (since encryption is negotiated regardless of any certificate). But on the other hand, authenticating the server (as in the endpoint of the connection, not the data it serves) is what ultimately prevents people from injecting ads or "other stuff" when they really want.

Yes, I too would love the ability to install TLS CAs that are scoped to a single domain subtree (like how it is possible with OpenSSH's certificates), or at least wider support of 'nameConstraints' (the extension that truly restricts a CA to only your domain and which half the things happily ignore). But unfortunately we're not even at the point yet where most Linux software could distinguish basic trust purposes - only Mozilla's NSS has distinct "trusted for TLS" and "trusted for S/MIME", and p11-kit has been *trying* to expose that to the broader ecosystem, but most software is still at the caveman level of "everything in ca-certificates.pem is trusted permanently for every purpose"... > I've been considering that option. I'm not experienced enough in OpenSSL to have a CA myself, but I'd consider eventually having one. Of course, I'd like to restrict it to emitting certificates for my domains only, and I'd sign the CA itself with my PGP key, but indeed, it would be an improvement over what I'm doing now. Honestly OpenSSL's own tooling isn't great, it has an "openssl ca" but its usability is, ehh. The "easy-rsa" script that comes with OpenVPN might be an improvement. For a GUI, the Qt-based XCA seemed alright as well. (Smallstep (step-ca) also seems relatively popular but it is Infrastructure, not a standalone tool. It didn't quite click for me; I ended up writing my own CA in Ruby's openssl libraries, then another using python-certbuilder, then another using python-cryptography...) > The reason I provide TLS is not for authenticating my server (I don't consider it authentic myself), but rather for encrypting (at least part of) the requests and responses, so that people sniffing (and perhaps injecting adds or other stuff) have it at least more difficult. FWIW, most (all?) GNU projects GPG-sign their release tarballs and release git tags. For GNU coreutils and Gnulib, our repository is mirrored in many places, some automatically syncing from Savannah and some not. So, if this issue were abused, it certainly wouldn't be good, but it wouldn't be unrecoverable. Anyways, it is very refreshing to see a software security company disclose these issues responsibly, and follow it up with an article that is not condescending to the project in discussion and which voices their good intentions: > Like much of the infrastructure free software depends on, it’s run by a handful of volunteers and FSF staff with limited resources. We wanted to put our resources to work there. Many thanks to them for that, and for catching these issues.

This sounds like git commits are not necessarily signed; is there a technical or operational reason for this? Because I imagine that you could use such a backdoor to subtly inject or rewrite commits, and those changes would inadvertently end up inside the signed tarballs as well?

Even with SHA-1, this is not feasible. While the collision resistance of SHA-1 is broken and you can craft special pairs of inputs that share the same arbitrary hash, the pre-image resistance still is comparatively solid – finding a different input for a given hash is still not practical.

There are some attacks for very long messages (2^100 operations for 2^60 bytes), but for the given scenario "commit hashes unchanged [aka given] and the diffs relatively similar", there are no known attacks against SHA-1. We still should probably switch to SHA-2 sooner than later nonetheless; but for this specific requirement, SHA-1 is still more than strong enough for now.

While the collision resistance of SHA-1 is broken and you can craft special pairs of inputs that share the same arbitrary hash, ...

So this just adds one more layer to the attack. Before you change the git repository you need to craft this pair of commits, one with a genuine bug fix that you sneak into the repository and another one additionally containing an evil payload. Once you have access to the repository you can switch out the commits.

Yes, this sounds far fetched, but not so much after the xz utils attack.

We still should probably switch to SHA-2 sooner than later nonetheless;

Well, neither commit it going to look normal. There's going to be 128 binary bytes in there as the algorithm tries to make two files with the same hash. Then they have a common suffix. So the good and evil payload exist in both commits, you just have to find 128 bytes which are somehow going to select the evil or the good payload. In the actual attack it involved a file with a pdf and an embedded jpeg. In pdf there is lots of room to hide stuff, in source code not so much. A chosen prefix attack would be more dangerous but AFAIK does not exist. Besides the fact that GitHub (and other libraries) have code to detect this attack.

If you have A-B-[you merge C]-C'-[others pull]-[others push]-[you pull because others pushed], you will be the only one who has a diverging history. Now, if that is a problem depends on your git config – if you have pull.ff, git will abort; but if you have pull.rebase or pull.no-rebase, you need to be rather vigilant to notice anything.

As an attacker, I probably would also try to insert a new commit instead of rewriting one; but on the other hand if you know that people are using (no-)rebase, a silent rewrite would be really hard to detect afterwards. And (no-)rebase is not super uncommon in my experience, because depending on how you or your team work, feature branches are not necessarily linear.

If I were an attacker, I think crafting an evil Merge remote-branch 'master' into 'my-topic' commit which adds the evil content among a sea of "sync" changes in a contribution would be a juicy target. Especially in squash merge workflows.

I really need to finish the "reject up-merges" check to ban such "wrong way" merges…but any merge commit is ripe for abuse. At least in the standard forge-based flows. Email, Gerrit, and other per-patch mechanisms would be "immune" from it just by the fact that they don't handle merge commit contributions like that.

The default Git setup on Savannah--or at least groff's--is configured to not allow force pushes at all. That's a little frustrating for me, because I'd prefer to have public "feature branches" or, for example right now, a "post-1.25" branch since we're in a (sort of) code freeze for the 1.25.0 release. But for the way I work, there's no point having a feature branch if I can't rewrite its history aggressively, because I make lots of mistakes and change my mind frequently. I think I asked once if force-pushes could be enabled for certain branches, but I don't recall ever getting an answer. But if this policy keeps Savannah safer from a supply-chain attack, I won't grumble.

#9991. Measuring benchmark optimization in speech recognition

Public voice AI benchmarks increasingly suggest that models are performing at human levels. Yet those scores don't always reflect how models work in the real-world. Since public benchmarks are open and widely used, models can also become optimized for the tests themselves. Their scores may improve because they have learned benchmark-specific patterns and not because they have become better at the underlying task.

One reason is that traditional benchmarks overlook many of the conditions and qualities that make voice systems reliable, natural, contextually appropriate, and effective in practice. That's why we recently introduced held-out sets in Real World VoiceEQ, the Open-ASR Leaderboard, and the Far-field ASR Leaderboard: to measure more of what matters in real-world use.

However, broader measurement alone does not solve the problem. This phenomenon, sometimes called benchmark optimization or "benchmaxxing," is often discussed around machine learning, however, it has been difficult to measure in speech recognition.

Our latest research introduces three tests to help quantify it. We evaluated 11 widely used open-source ASR models and found that several of the highest-scoring systems reproduced benchmark transcripts from the VoxPopuli English and LibriSpeech (clean, other) datasets – even when the audio contradicted them, relevant words had been silenced, or the audio equally supported two different written forms.

In some cases, models appeared to rely not only on what was said, but also on subtle acoustic cues that indicated which benchmark they were being tested on. As a result, their scores overstated how well they could transcribe speech more generally.

VoxPopuli is known to contain a high number of transcription errors (which is why Artificial Analysis released a cleaned version). Our consensus disagreement probe tests what happens when leading ASR models encounter these errors: Do they accurately transcribe what the audio says, or reproduce the benchmark's incorrect reference transcript?

To test this at scale, we use an ensemble of independent models selected for their low phoneme error rate (PER). PER measures how closely a written transcription matches the sounds in the audio, making it a useful proxy for how faithfully a model transcribes what it hears. The ensemble results can be used to flag cases in which the models unanimously disagree with the benchmark's reference transcript. We then compare a sample of those flagged cases against human annotations to validate the corrected transcripts.

For example, one VoxPopuli clip audibly includes the phrase "Thank you, Mr. President," but the reference transcript omits "Thank you." Six of the 11 models we tested reproduced the benchmark's erroneous transcript—giving the "expected" answer even though it contradicted the audio. On the real clip, the formatting follows the same pattern: models that omit "Thank you" also reproduce the benchmark's punctuation style, writing "Mr" without a period, while models that include the audible phrase tend to write "Mr." with the period.

When we present the same content in newly collected voices from EU parliamentary recordings or generic voices, this behavior often weakens or disappears. In the below samples, all but one model flips back to transcribing the audio-faithful transcript for a clone of a new parliamentary recording. This suggests that the models are responding to acoustic cues that help them identify the benchmark membership and thus produce the expected transcript even if it contradicts the audio.

The reference transcript for this clip reads "Mr President, I have another complaint about this procedure, which is that it is not secret." The audio in all three clips below actually says the same thing, preceded by an audible "Thank you,"—the clones are text-to-speech renditions of that true sentence, so the courtesy is audible in all three. Green highlighting and ✅ mark a transcript that includes the audible "Thank you"; red highlighting and ❌ mark a transcript that reproduces the benchmark's erroneous omission. All transcripts are raw model output, prior to any normalization—casing and punctuation are preserved exactly as generated, including lowercase output from some models.

Clone of a parliament speaker recorded after every model's training cutoff

Parakeet is the only model that flips between reproducing the benchmark on the real clip and getting it right on the same-speaker clone. Phi-4 is the only model still dropping the courtesy on the ep-fresh clone. When we instead resynthesize the sentence in a generic TTS voice unconnected to any parliamentary recording, all eleven models restore the courtesy.

The results suggest that this problem is both widespread and meaningful. Our methodology flagged potential reference errors in 40% of the VoxPopuli test clips we analyzed, affecting roughly 3% of all reference words.

Models exhibiting benchmark-optimized behavior reproduced erroneous reference transcripts 18–30% of the time. The scatterplot below compares VoxPopuli word error rate (WER) on the x-axis with the rate at which each model reproduces the benchmark's incorrect reference instead of the consensus correction. The models with the lowest WER—and therefore the strongest reported benchmark performance—are also the most likely to reproduce these errors.

To build on the consensus disagreement probe, we deliberately silence numbers in the audio samples of test datasets and ask the models to transcribe what it hears. The number is literally absent from the audio, so models should not output any number, much less the exact number in the text.

Some of these numbers are semi-predictable (although still unlikely for a model to predict), yet others are quite surprising. The following clip combines both probes, showing both how models recreate reference transcript errors including an incorrect number and one model even autocompletes a relatively random year (2011) despite it being silenced. In each model's row below:

Recovery rates were highest on the public benchmarks and lower on held-out or newly collected audio (ep-fresh and libri-fresh below). On LibriSpeech, some of the strongest benchmark-performing models reproduced masked numbers in roughly 30–40% of examples, even though the number itself had been removed. The effect weakened on freshly collected data for several models, suggesting that the surrounding benchmark-associated audio—not only textual autocomplete—helped the models recover the reference.

Our orthographic switching probe tests whether models reproduce the exact spelling used in a benchmark's reference transcript despite it not being clear in the audio. Orthographic variants are words that are semantically and phonetically identical but can be spelled different ways (1 vs one, Mr. vs mister, John vs Jon, Honor vs Honour, etc). In theory, models should consistently prefer one spelling over another, or alternate between them at roughly random rates. If models systematically switch to match what is in each benchmark's reference transcript, that suggests the models are picking up on which spelling the test expects.

Transcription: "I URGED ON THE BOYS THAT WHATEVER HAPPENED WE SHOULD NOT SHOOT ANY ONE" — models using "any one": 6/11, models using "anyone": 5/11

Transcription: "CAMOUFLAGE WAS NOT A WORD THE CAPTAIN OR ANYONE ELSE OF HIS TIME YET UNDERSTOOD" — models using "any one": 2/11, models using "anyone": 9/11

Within LibriSpeech, we test one intra-dataset switch involving an older spacing convention: some reference transcripts use "any one", while others use "anyone." We measure the minimum accuracy for a given variant, which we call "switch rate". If a model only uses one variant it would have a 0% switch rate; a model which picks randomly would be expected to have a 50% switch rate. A model which knows which variant to use in every test sample would earn a 100% switch rate.

Our second probe tests an inter-dataset switch, in which each benchmark uses a different spelling convention consistently across its test corpus. For example, VoxPopuli uses the abbreviation "Mr.," while LibriSpeech spells out "Mister."

Multiple models exceed the 50% random-choice baseline, with some reaching roughly 90% switch accuracy. This suggests that the models can identify which dataset an audio sample comes from and select the spelling convention that benchmark expects, even though both forms sound identical.

To test whether these behaviors generalize beyond the public benchmarks, we also collected fresh data from the same source domains but after the models' training cutoffs: recent European Parliament recordings for VoxPopuli and recordings from newly active LibriVox narrators for LibriSpeech. However, when presented with recently collected data from the same domain, many models stop matching the reference transcript and revert to more audio faithful transcriptions.

Other interventions point to the same conclusion. Phrases which are present in the audio but are omitted in the reference transcript can reappear when a model is asked to translate the audio or when its attention is restricted to the relevant frames. Trimming away surrounding benchmark context, or appending ordinary conversational audio, can also restore the faithful transcript. Appending VoxPopuli audio can have the opposite effect, making otherwise faithful synthetic or mined samples more likely to match the benchmark reference.

Together, these results suggest that models are able to faithfully transcribe the literal spoken words, but are using surrounding acoustic context to decide whether to follow the audio or a benchmark-specific transcription policy.

Our findings suggest that, on two major open-source datasets, some models detect dataset-associated acoustic cues and adjust their transcription behavior accordingly. Specifically, models may reproduce words that are absent from the audio but present in the reference transcript, recover silenced numbers at elevated rates, or use surrounding acoustic context to select the written variant expected by a particular benchmark.

For people selecting models, these findings underscore the importance of using fully held-out evaluation sets, as RW-Voice-EQ Bench and the Open ASR Leaderboard do, and of looking beyond word error rate on a single public benchmark. To this end, a "Benchmark fitting" tab has been added to the Open ASR Leaderboard, which includes two of the above analyses across all models: quantifying (1) reference error rates from VoxPopuli and (2) orthographic switching across all public datasets. The relevant scripts are open-sourced on GitHub as well as the un-normalized model outputs.

Our findings also suggest that benchmark developers should avoid simple independent and identically distributed test splits in favor of temporal, speaker, or other metadata-based separation. Greater transparency around training data and model-selection procedures would also help researchers understand how these behaviors arise.

Public benchmarks remain valuable: they are transparent, repeatable, easy to run, and well understood by the research community. But they are most useful when we can distinguish genuine transcription improvements from benchmark-specific gains that do not generalize to new audio.

For more information, we encourage you to read our full report.

#9990. Announcing NetBSD 11.1

Download 11.1 from our CDN: amd64 USB, amd64 DVD, i386 USB, i386 CD-ROM, sparc64 DVD, sparc64 CD-ROM, macppc CD-ROM, RISC-V devices, Cavium Octeon MIPS devices, Nintendo Wii, various Arm devices, full release dir with everything else.

Hashes, signed with the NetBSD Security Officer's PGP key, of all files in the distribution.

The NetBSD Project is pleased to announce NetBSD 11.1, the first point release of the NetBSD 11 stable branch.

An existing installation can be upgraded by booting an installation image and selecting the Upgrade option.

If you are using other update methods, update the kernel and modules first, then reboot and update your userspace.

This release primarily focuses on security and bug fixes, since our aim was to get it released as soon as possible to address certain security issues.

The complete list of changes can be found in the CHANGES and CHANGES-11.1 files in the top level directory of the NetBSD 11.1 release tree.

Complete source and binaries for NetBSD 11.1 are available for download at many sites around the world. You can download NetBSD 11.1 from our main CDN, or use a mirror site close to you. A list of hashes, signed by the NetBSD Security Officer's PGP key, is available for the NetBSD 11.1 distribution in this file.

NetBSD is free. All of the code is under non-restrictive licenses, and may be used without paying royalties to anyone. Free support services are available via our mailing lists and website. Commercial support is available from a variety of sources. More extensive information on NetBSD is available from our website:

The NetBSD 11.1 release provides supported binary distributions for the following systems:

Ports included in the release but not fully supported or functional:

The NetBSD Foundation would like to thank all those who have contributed code, hardware, documentation, funds, colocation for our servers, web pages and other documentation, release engineering, and other resources over the years. More information on the people who make NetBSD happen is available at:

NetBSD is a free, fast, secure, and highly portable Unix-like Open Source operating system. It is available for a wide range of platforms, from large-scale servers and powerful desktop systems to handheld and embedded devices. Its clean design and advanced features make it excellent for use in both production and research environments, and the source code is freely available under a business-friendly license. NetBSD is developed and supported by a large and vibrant international community. Many applications are readily available through pkgsrc, the NetBSD Packages Collection.

The NetBSD Foundation was chartered in 1995, with the task of overseeing core NetBSD project services, promoting the project within industry and the open source community, and holding intellectual property rights on much of the NetBSD code base. Day-to-day operations of the project are handled by volunteers.

As a non-profit organization with no commercial backing, the NetBSD Foundation depends on donations from its users, and we would like to ask you to consider making a donation to the NetBSD Foundation in support of continuing production of our fine operating system. Your generous donation would be particularly welcome to help with ongoing upgrades and maintenance, as well as with operating expenses for the NetBSD Foundation.

Donations can be done via PayPal to , or via Google Checkout and are fully tax-deductible in the US. See www.NetBSD.org/donations/ for more information, or contact directly.

#9989. What We Missed: Feds Lasso Texas Laptop Farms

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

In this video, Dark Reading editors discuss some of the news they didn't get a chance to cover, from busting up North Korea's stateside infrastructure in "Operation Lonestar Justice" to Staples' gift card bonanza.

The US government is striking back against the ever-persistent threat of fake IT worker schemes run by the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK).

In this episode of "What We Missed," Dark Reading's Rob Wright and Alex Culafi discuss some of the recent news events and topics that didn't make it into the publication, starting with FBI raids across more than 40 Texas residences that were allegedly running "laptop farms."

The law-enforcement action, dubbed “Operation Lonestar Roundup,” seized 187 devices, charged 14 people, and arrested individuals accused of facilitating North Korean threat actors running fake IT worker schemes. The schemes disrupted by Operation Lonestar Roundup impacted more than 70 US companies, according to the FBI.

Fake IT worker schemes typically involve DPRK actors masquerading as IT professionals and developers, either using fake or stolen identities, to gain employment at US companies. The threat actors then use their positions to exfiltrate sensitive data, steal intellectual property, and gather intelligence.

Related:Ex-OpenAI Engineer Detained After Planting Secret Recorder at HQ

Also discussed on this episode: Russian police arrested alleged members of a cybercriminal group known as the "DataSuckers," which has taken credit for several breaches against companies in Russia and Ukraine; and according to a report from 404 Media, a Chinese criminal operation breached Staples' internal customer support system and used it to issue thousands of gift cards, worth $5 million.

For all of our Dark Reading news videos, please check out our YouTube channel and our curated video articles.

This transcript has been edited for clarity and length by Informa TechTarget's internal AI assistant. For the full experience, please watch the video.

Rob Wright is a longtime reporter with more than 25 years of experience as a technology journalist. Prior to joining Dark Reading as senior news director, he spent more than a decade at TechTarget's SearchSecurity in various roles, including senior news director, executive editor and editorial director. Before that, he worked for several years at CRN, Tom's Hardware Guide, and VARBusiness Magazine covering a variety of technology beats and trends.

Prior to becoming a technology journalist in 2000, he worked as a weekly and daily newspaper reporter in Virginia, where he won three Virginia Press Association awards in 1998 and 1999. At TechTarget and Dark Reading, he has won several Azbee awards, including the 2026 National Silver Award for a series on vibe coding.

At Dark Reading, Rob currently covers security operations, cloud security, and Internet infrastructure. He has a keen interest in malvertising activity and the certificate authority industry, and has written extensively on both topics. He graduated from the University of Richmond in 1997 with a degree in journalism and English. A native of Massachusetts, he lives in the Boston area.

Alex is an award-winning writer, journalist, and podcast host based in Boston. After cutting his teeth writing for independent gaming publications as a teenager, he graduated from Emerson College in 2016 with a Bachelor of Science in journalism. He has previously been published on VentureFizz, Search Security, Nintendo World Report, and elsewhere.

At Dark Reading, he covers a variety of cybersecurity topics, including the cybercrime ecosystem, open source security, and the intersection between AI and threat actors. In his spare time, Alex hosts the weekly Nintendo podcast, "Talk Nintendo Podcast," and works on personal writing projects, including two previously self-published science fiction novels.

He has received numerous awards, including TechTarget's Writer of the Year in 2022 as well as more than 10 Azbee awards for his reporting between 2022 and today.

InfoQ Homepage Presentations Beyond the Harness: Canvas for AI Agents

Nimisha Asthagiri shares how applying proven product engineering and architecture principles creates a bounded canvas for AI agents. She explains how this model provides agents with bounded autonomy, continuous drift detection, and decision records to scale software development resiliently.

Nimisha Asthagiri is a Technical Advisor at Thoughtworks where she leads client digital transformations using design thinking, change management, and platform architecture. Her current focus is architecting agentic enterprises with systems thinking for responsible AI.

QCon AI is a practitioner-led event focused entirely on the engineering discipline required to scale these workloads safely. It provides direct access to the architectural playbooks and failure metrics that peer organizations use in production.
