#9870. Investors Dish on New Startups & What They'd Back Next

News, news analysis, and commentary on the latest trends in cybersecurity technology.

The cybersecurity market is difficult to predict, but a glimpse into the annual DataTribe Challenge shows what's trending and what's not.

Startups have been battling it out on the DataTribe Challenge stage for the past nine years, but this year's event still saw some firsts.

A cyber insurance company made the top five finalists, and attendees got to vote for their favorite finalist with the People's Choice Award. Both of these firsts highlighted how people are looking for answers to new risks introduced by artificial intelligence (AI).

The DataTribe Challenge, hosted by the cyber startup foundry and venture capital firm, is one of the signature events of its annual Cyber Innovation Conference. The meeting, which took place in October, aims to unite the cybersecurity ecosystem, from founders to investors and — since it's held in Washington, D.C. — some policymakers, too.

Cybersecurity conferences pop up on the calendar more frequently these days; that momentum is important "to keep the information fresh" as the industry and threat landscape transforms rapidly, explains Robert Ackerman, co-founder and managing partner at DataTribe. Game-changing incidents that require sharing information emerge almost daily now, he adds, pointing to the more recent PHP2Shell vulnerability that attackers jumped on and proved difficult for organizations to patch.

Related:AI Agents as Insider Threats: Inside Microsoft's Bet on a Unified Security Stack

An expanding pool of cyber-related startups is also driving industry transformation. Nearly 700 rising companies submitted entries or were considered for this year's Challenge, which pairs startups with mentors before they pitch to judges who crown the winner.

As Ackerman and Leo Scott, managing director at DataTribe, filtered down the contestants into the top five list, they found it interesting that many of the startups focused on the dynamics around how AI is driving the market as organizations transition from AI adoption to managing the technology.

Some companies had a more direct tie. This year's winner, Sondera, aims to solve agentic architecture challenges like improving guardrails and security controls.

But cyber insurance company Navasana, which made the top five for the first time ever, was an example of a company indirectly focused on AI. Instead, Navasana launched to handle new risk dynamics that AI created, speaking to broader industry trends.

At one level, everyone's been thinking about cyber insurance for a long time, Ackerman adds. But looking at how policies are written in cyber, he has noticed a shift in risk as they add disclaimers and exemptions.

"What makes cyber attractive from an investment perspective is you never really solve it," Ackerman tells Dark Reading. "You never mitigate risk fully. It's a very hard puzzle piece to put together. The hope with AI is you get this real-time data to understand posture and environments. I still think there's a real lag though because insurance doesn't operate in real time."

Related:RemoteThreat Bets Security Teams Need to Test What Happens After Defenses Fail

Navasna marked the first cyber insurer to make the top five due to the end-to-end, continuous services it offers in a space where organizations manage such a broad umbrella of needs. As an early-stage investor, Ackerman is not looking to "feed the consensus machine" but wants to anticipate what's next. In venture capital, that's hard right now, he adds. Still, the conference and DataTribe Challenge look to showcase companies that are currently topical and addressing real needs.

Navasana is an example of more emerging needs, says Ackerman, while Sondera is in the "sweet spot" by addressing current challenges, as attacks make it clear that agentic AI needs more guardrails.

Sondera is "doing some really interesting things in that space that are well beyond what others are doing," says Scott. What resonated with the audience was how much research Sondera put into understanding what organizations actually need, he adds.

Rather than operating at the rule level, Sondera's approach starts at a much higher level, beginning with the human's underlying intent and what they're trying to achieve. Then organizations can work with users to generate the specific rules.

Related:Deception by Design: CISA's Guide to Tricking Cybercriminals

It's increasingly evident that agents can be very persistent and act independently, so control is essential. That may be one reason that Sondera took home the trophy — people really understand the problems they've seen in their environments, Ackerman adds.

Ackerman sees two timelines in cybersecurity right now. Discussions over the past 18 to 24 months centered around concerns that offense has more of an advantage as attackers use AI to become faster and more advanced. Defense will catch up, but he believes that what the industry knows about cybersecurity — how to protect systems, and layer defense and zero trust — still work.

"We just have to apply them efficiently all the time," he urges.

The other timeline is what happens after 24 months. What issues will emerge then? Those are the core concepts, like protecting Internet infrastructure, that DataTribe wants to showcase in these events.

And the long-term lens is what the investors are betting on right now.

"It's not about what is going to get picked up in the next three to four months," Ackerman says. The startups and investments "have more of a five- to 10-year time horizon," he says.

One of Ackerman's favorite pastimes once startups wrap up their Challenge pitches is to walk around the floor while everyone's waiting for the judges to cast their votes and announce the winner. He considers the disconnect: He has spent weeks with the companies, coaching and prepping, yet the audience full of people from across the industry only get to know them for 20 minutes.

That's what makes storytelling so important, not just the cybersecurity and technical points. Learning what the judges and audience think of these companies is important for DataTribe, as well as for the startups which is the true value of cyber competitions.

For Ackerman, it's always great to hear that people had been thinking about a problem one of the contestants was trying to solve, but no one had developed a solution.

"That's validating," Ackerman says. "We're sort of directionally correct, which maybe in this market is the best you can do on any given day."

Arielle spent the last decade working as a reporter, transitioning from human interest stories to covering all things cybersecurity related in 2020. Now, as a features writer for Dark Reading, she delves into the security problems enterprises face daily, providing context and actionable steps. She looks for stories that go past the initial news to understand where the industry is going. Her coverage areas include identity and access management, cyber risk and operations, industrial control systems, operational technology, and ransomware trends.

She previously lived in Florida where she wrote for the Tampa Bay Times before returning to Boston where her cybersecurity career took off at TechTarget SearchSecurity. When she's not writing about cybersecurity, she pursues personal projects that include a mystery novel and poetry collection.

NVIDIA’s DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017-NVFP4 is a quantized, multimodal MoE language model intended for deployment in agent systems, chatbots, RAG, and other AI applications. It is based on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 and uses a Causal Encoder-Decoder architecture with Compressed Sparse Attention 2. Maintainer: nvidia. The stated license is MIT; the source describes commercial and non-commercial use.

Text and image input with text generation; chatbot and RAG applications; AI-agent deployments, including tool calling through the documented vLLM configuration. Evaluation covers scientific reasoning, long-context recall, scientific coding, instruction following, visual understanding, and terminal-based agent tasks.

The base model may produce biased or toxic responses, inaccuracies, omissions, or irrelevant and redundant text. This checkpoint requires a vLLM build with MXFP4 Engram support; stock vLLM images cannot load its Engram tables, and SGLang has not been validated. Speculative decoding was not exercised. Validate the intended runtime and application with task-specific testing. The source reports benchmark results but does not establish that this checkpoint is superior overall to its source-precision baseline.

The supplied related model DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-NVFP4 is a different version: its name omits the 1017 suffix, so do not assume its checkpoint or results are interchangeable. Against the stated MXFP4 source baseline, this checkpoint's reported scores were 92.93 vs. 92.77 on GPQA Diamond, 80.19 vs. 80.41 on AA-LCR, 57.32 vs. 57.58 on SciCode, 76.47 vs. 76.33 on IFBench, 78.73 vs. 78.38 on MMMU-Pro, and 81.11 vs. 81.81 on Terminal-Bench 2.1. These are benchmark-specific results, not evidence of a general winner.

Transformer model, DeepseekV41ForCausalLM; Causal Encoder-Decoder MoE with Compressed Sparse Attention 2. The backbone has 552B total parameters, with 8B activated during prefill and 16B during decode, plus 196B Engram conditional memory. Quantization uses Model Optimizer v0.48.0rc0: routed expert weights and activations are NVFP4 W4A4, group size 16; Engram lookup tables are MXFP4. Other components retain source precision, including MXFP8 where applicable. Expert weight conversion preserved dequantized values, while Engram conversion is lossy; this does not guarantee identical inference outputs. The checkpoint is about 400 GiB in 48 safetensors shards. Supported hardware is NVIDIA Blackwell; preferred OS is Linux. Reported inference used vLLM on four NVIDIA GB300 GPUs. Evaluation scores are percentages: MXFP4 source / this NVFP4 checkpoint—GPQA Diamond 92.77 / 92.93; AA-LCR 80.41 / 80.19; SciCode 57.58 / 57.32; IFBench 76.33 / 76.47; MMMU-Pro 78.38 / 78.73; Terminal-Bench 2.1 81.81 / 81.11. Training data details are undisclosed. Calibration used 1,024 samples total from CNN/DailyMail and selected Nemotron-Post-Training-Dataset-v2 subsets.

Text and images; image input is specified as RGB. The model card states a context length of up to 1 million tokens. Text and image input were validated with the documented vLLM command. Tool calling can be enabled with the listed vLLM flags.

Text strings, generated as one-dimensional sequences.

Use a vLLM build with MXFP4 Engram support; stock vLLM images cannot load this checkpoint. The documented command was used with four GB300 GPUs. For tool calling, add --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser deepseek_v41.

Q: What runtime does this checkpoint support?

A: The supplied documentation supports vLLM with MXFP4 Engram support. Stock vLLM images cannot load the checkpoint's Engram lookup tables; SGLang has not been validated.

Q: What hardware and operating system are specified?

A: NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs and Linux are specified. Reported inference used four NVIDIA GB300 GPUs.

A: Yes. The documented inputs include text and RGB images, and both text and image input were validated with the stated vLLM command.

A: The model card states a context length of up to 1 million tokens.

Q: Does the checkpoint support tool calling?

A: The vLLM usage notes specify enabling it with --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser deepseek_v41.

A: The supplied model information states MIT and describes commercial and non-commercial use.

Q: Are speculative decoding and SGLang validated?

A: No. Speculative decoding was not exercised, and SGLang has not been validated with this checkpoint.

#9868. PapRAT Cyber-Espionage Campaign Leaves a 'Bitter' Taste in South Asia

Organizations in the region face growing cyberattacks from the known India-linked threat group, which leverages legitimate Windows functionality in three distinct attack chains.

A known South Asian cyber-espionage group has been targeting organizations across the region with attacks designed to compromise Windows systems, establish persistence, and give attackers remote control over infected machines using custom malware.

The attacks, attributed "with high confidence" to the South Asian threat group known as Bitter (aka TA397), involve three distinct infection chains and demonstrate the group's expanding malware capabilities, according to new research from FortiGuard Labs published today.

Bitter, one of several threat groups linked to India, has been active since at least 2013 and has historically targeted government, energy, and engineering organizations. The group is known for using tailored attack campaigns to gain persistent access to victim networks, collect information, and maintain remote control over compromised systems.

At the center of the latest threat campaign is PapRAT, a custom remote access Trojan (RAT) that gives attackers extensive control over compromised Windows systems, including the ability to execute commands, manipulate files, capture screenshots, and download additional payloads, according to FortiGuard Labs.

Related:Philippine Migrant Worker Data Likely Leaked in 69GB Government Breach

"This campaign illustrates how Bitter combines native Windows tools with custom malware to establish and maintain access to targeted systems," Cara Lin, a FortiGuard Labs threat researcher, wrote in the post.

Bitter has recently revamped PapRAT from a C++ code base to Rust, expanding its functionality in the process from eight commands to 11, according to the report. Additional capabilities in the latest version include PowerShell execution, a sleep directive, and a clean-exit command.

"PapRAT's C++ and Rust implementations indicate continued investment in Bitter's toolset," Lin wrote.

Indeed, attackers have increasingly adopted Rust for malware development for various reasons, including its cross-platform development capabilities and potential evasion advantages.

The latest updates to PapRAT also underscore the importance of certain defensive measures, including "monitoring malicious behavior across scripting tools, scheduled tasks, and installer activity alongside detecting known malware signatures," Lin wrote.

Researchers observed three distinct attack chains being used by Bitter, all of which exploit legitimate Windows functionality to disguise malicious behavior.

These tactics demonstrate "how advanced cyberespionage operations deliberately abuse native system tools to evade traditional endpoint detection," notes Shane Barney, chief information security officer at Keeper Security.

Related:One Compromised Laptop, Billions Lost: The Binance Attack-Path Warning

The first attack chain uses a malicious LNK file that abuses the native Windows ftp.exe utility to execute scripts and create scheduled tasks that maintain contact with the attackers' command-and-control (C2) server.

The second uses a VHDX disk image containing an LNK file that opens a decoy spreadsheet while silently launching an MSI installer to deploy PapRAT.

The third attack begins with a URL shortcut that retrieves an LNK file through WebDAV, leading to an MSI installer that deploys PapRAT. In this chain, PapRAT also delivers WmRAT, a secondary implant previously documented by other researchers, according to FortiGuard Labs.

"By co-opting native Windows utilities like ftp.exe and scheduled tasks to establish initial command-and-control communication, threat actors operate within trusted administrative channels before deploying custom malware," Barney observes. "When an intrusion leverages trusted system processes, signature-based controls simply have nothing to alert on."

This so-called "hybrid tradecraft," which combines legitimate Windows functionality with custom malware, requires organizations to focus on strict privilege boundaries and identity security rather than relying on endpoint signatures alone as part of a comprehensive defense strategy, Barney says.

Related:Microsoft's AI Risk Report Misses This Key Detail

To defend against these attacks, organizations should treat unexpected LNK files, URL shortcuts, disk images, and MSI packages with caution, particularly when delivered through unsolicited messages, Lin recommended in the post.

"Combining user awareness with controls that detect suspicious execution chains and outbound C2 traffic can help limit exposure to campaigns that blend legitimate Windows functionality with custom malware," she wrote.

The third attack chain is particularly problematic for defenders because removing PapRAT from compromised systems may not eliminate the attacker's access, observes Jason Soroko, senior fellow at Sectigo.

This means defenders need to look deeper into their systems "to check what else was installed and identify scripts and scheduled tasks that could keep fetching commands," he says. A comprehensive recovery effort must look beyond the file that triggered the original alert to identify any additional payloads, persistence mechanisms, or other components of the compromise.

#9866. Normalizing a Wide Well and Pipeline Telemetry Table Without Re-Ingesting History

Tiger Data, the creators of TimescaleDB, develops the open-source time-series database built on PostgreSQL.

Tiger Data, the creators of TimescaleDB, develops the open-source time-series database built on PostgreSQL.

Tiger Data, the creators of TimescaleDB, develops the open-source time-series database built on PostgreSQL.

An oilfield SCADA migration guide: reshape a wide sensor table into a narrow hypertable plus a metadata table, in place, with your dashboards still running.

Every new instrument the field commissions turns into a schema change for you. A casing-pressure transmitter goes on a pad, a flow computer lands on a gathering line, and your wide telemetry table gets another indexed column on top of years of readings. You already know the shape is wrong. What has kept you from fixing it is the cost of the fix: reshaping a table that size looks like re-ingesting all of that history, and the dashboards on top of it cannot go dark while you do.

This guide walks through that migration: moving a wide time-series table to a narrow schema in place, with history intact and dashboards still running. It leaves out the harder case of tags whose descriptors change over time, and it picks up where Time-Series Cardinality leaves off, so it does not re-argue the shape.

If you control both the ingest and the queries, there is a gentler route: run a second ingest into the new table alongside the old one, then move queries over one at a time. That breaks the migration into small, separately reversible steps, and it is worth taking when you can. This guide covers the common case where you can't, because the ingest can't be duplicated or the queries aren't yours to rewrite. If you are on Tiger Cloud and would rather not run it yourself, the Enterprise plan includes a migration team that will help design a migration plan around your own tables.

What you get at the end is a table that stops fighting you. Readings land in a narrow hypertable of (recorded_at, tag_id, value), so the next instrument the field adds becomes one row in a metadata table instead of a column across years of history. Every descriptor the wide table repeated on each reading now lives once, on the tag. And the dashboards you cannot take down keep working, because the old table name and the old columns survive as a view over the new shape. On a hundred million generated readings, the whole sequence took under seven minutes of machine time on our hardware, against a clean dataset with no live ingest competing for the disk; most of that was the reshape in Step 2.

Three things need to be true before you schedule it:

This is a typical wide origin table. Tables shaped like this rarely come from a commercial historian such as PI, which keeps tag metadata apart from the readings and does not store them in SQL at all. They come from in-house ingest, where a project starts with a few wells and a hand-written INSERT, then keeps growing as pads and instruments are added. Map your own columns onto it; the names below are the ones every later step uses.

The DDL is shown in the current table-option form. Yours was probably created with create_hypertable(), and that changes nothing below. If your origin is a plain Postgres table rather than a hypertable, the migration gets easier in exactly two places: Step 3 gets CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY back, and the rename in Step 4 is an ordinary Postgres rename. Everything else is identical.

Create the destination before you touch the origin. Two tables: the metadata table owns the descriptors, and the narrow hypertable owns the facts.

The shape itself is the standard one, and TigerData's metadata table best practices cover the reasoning; the cardinality piece measured the benefits. Three choices inside that DDL decide whether the narrow shape pays off.

Keep tag_id a narrow BIGINT surrogate. The text tag path goes in tag_name once, on the metadata row. A fat TEXT key repeated on every fact row forfeits most of the win.

Enforce referential integrity at the ingest layer. A foreign key from the facts to tag_metadata adds a per-row check on a high-ingest path, which is why the DDL above declares none. If you want the constraint anyway, the supported direction is a hypertable referencing a regular table, which is the direction drawn here.

Segment by tag_id. Compression segmented by the tag is where the narrow schema's advantage widens most, and a source identifier is the usual segmentby candidate.

One consequence of creating the table this way: columnstore is on by default, so TimescaleDB creates a columnstore policy automatically, set to convert any chunk older than one chunk interval on a daily schedule. Every historical slice you are about to load is older than that, so the policy would start converting chunks while Step 2 is still writing next to them. The docs' own guidance for backfilling while converting is to pause the policy until the load is done, because conversion contends for locks with any concurrent write to the same chunk. Pause it now and re-enable it once the verification checks pass.

Two things are deliberately absent from the DDL. There is no index on the narrow table yet; tsdb.create_default_indexes = false keeps TimescaleDB from adding one, and Step 3 builds the composite index after the load. And there is one value DOUBLE PRECISION column, which assumes every tag is a float. Industrial tags are not uniformly float. If yours carry booleans, state codes, or strings, the appendix at the end shows the typed-column variant of this schema and the three places it changes the steps. Make that call before you reshape.

The whole migration rests on one assumption about your data: that a tag's descriptors are functionally dependent on the tag, so a given tag is always on the same device, at the same site, on the same line, reporting the same unit. The original post closes by asking you to check one property of your data before you plan anything. This is that check. Its answer decides whether the migration is an afternoon or a project. One scan, and it took about a minute against a hundred million rows.

An empty result is the clean case: every tag has carried exactly one descriptor set across its whole history, the backfill in Step 1 falls straight out of the data, and the rest of this guide is for you.

Rows mean some tags changed descriptors over their lifetime. On a pad this is routine. A workover moves a transmitter from one well to another, an instrument swap changes the device behind a tag path, or an RTU firmware upgrade bumps firmware_ver on every tag it serves. Those tags need availability windows, which is what the ts_start and ts_end columns in the metadata table exist for: one metadata row per descriptor set, bounded in time, with ts_last_seen tracking which row is current. That path makes the reshape join in Step 2 time-dependent and materially slower, and it is a longer migration, not just a different INSERT. This guide does not walk it; a follow-up will. If Step 0 returns rows, stop here and scope that migration instead of forcing this one.

One scan of the wide table, one row per tag. The text tag path lands in tag_name, and the surrogate is generated.

The guard is NOT EXISTS rather than ON CONFLICT ... DO NOTHING, and the difference matters. Both make the backfill safe to re-run, which Step 2 depends on. Only NOT EXISTS leaves Step 0's safety net armed: a tag that somehow carries two descriptor sets still trips the UNIQUE constraint on tag_name loudly, where ON CONFLICT would swallow it in silence and keep whichever set it saw first.

The pattern is a control table plus one transaction per time slice, where each transaction writes both the facts and its own completion marker. One unbounded INSERT ... SELECT over a multi-terabyte hypertable is the wrong instinct at this size, because a backfill this large cannot afford one long transaction: it holds a lock for hours, generates write-ahead log faster than replicas can consume it, and cannot resume if it dies at 90 percent.

A control table, rather than a unique constraint on (tag_id, recorded_at), records completions because that constraint would be expensive at this scale and may not even hold in field telemetry. A week is a reasonable slice width for a table this size; pick whatever keeps one transaction to minutes on your hardware.

The primary key on slice_start covers both ways a slice can be run twice. Retry a slice that already completed and the control-row insert fails on the key, taking the facts written in the same transaction down with it: nothing duplicated, one wasted slice of work. Kill a slice mid-run, as we did in the drill, and the transaction rolls back whole, no control row is written, and the retry starts from a clean slice.

The inner join silently drops any tag missing from tag_metadata, with no error and no warning, and a tag that first appears after Step 1's backfill is exactly such a tag. That is what the registration freeze in the prerequisites is for. If you cannot hold the freeze, re-run Step 1 before each slice; the NOT EXISTS guard makes that free.

How you drive the loop is the other trap. Ask the control table which windows are missing, and never track a MAX(slice_end) high-water mark, which steps straight over holes left by parallel slices or a crashed run.

Feed that list to whatever runs your slices, in parallel if you like, and the loop is done when it returns nothing. Stop one slice short of the present, though. Ingest is still landing in the wide table until the swap in Step 4, so the slice that contains now is incomplete by construction. Run it last, after the cutover, with sensor_readings_old as the source, because by then that table receives no writes and the slice is final. Never re-run a completed slice without first deleting its rows and its control row, or every fact in the window lands twice.

Build the indexes after the bulk load, not before. The load runs materially faster without an index to maintain, and the resulting B-tree is denser. The live-table reflex, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, is not supported on hypertables. The substitute is a one-line table option that builds the index one chunk per transaction.

One transaction per chunk means inserts into other chunks keep running while the index builds. If your read path has time-only scans with no tag predicate, add a plain (recorded_at DESC) index in the same step, since the DDL disabled the default one.

This only goes wrong if the build is interrupted, by a cancel, a crash, or an error partway through. Then the root index is marked invalid, with some chunks indexed and some not. It keeps working and still applies to new chunks; only the chunks the build missed go without it. To guarantee full coverage, find it, drop it, and rebuild:

Then ANALYZE both sensor_readings_narrow and tag_metadata. The join the compatibility view is about to put on the read path is exactly the plan that needs fresh statistics, and the planner has not seen a row of either table yet.

A rename is cheap in Postgres because tables are identified by OID rather than name, so ALTER TABLE ... RENAME TO is a metadata operation whatever the table's size, and hypertables rename the same way. Renaming alone is still not a non-breaking cutover. The rename preserves the table's name, not its shape. The narrow table has three columns where the old one had eight, so every query selecting site or line fails the moment the swap commits. A view restores the old shape under the old name, and the dashboards never learn the table moved.

The lock_timeout is not optional. The rename takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE. If one long-running read is in flight, the rename queues behind it, every later reader queues behind the rename, and a metadata operation turns into an outage. In a live two-session test, a three-second lock_timeout fired on schedule against a single held-open read instead of queueing behind it. Set it short and expect to retry during a quiet minute. The CREATE VIEW sits inside the same transaction on purpose: between the rename committing and the view existing there is no sensor_readings at all, and one short transaction closes that gap.

The view is a join on the read path, and the cardinality piece measured what that join costs against querying the narrow table directly: about two percent on the rollups and below measurement noise on the sub-millisecond queries. The view is read-path only, so repoint your ingest at sensor_readings_narrow explicitly rather than through an INSTEAD OF trigger. In practice that is the ingest service writing (recorded_at, tag_id, value) with the surrogate resolved from tag_metadata, as soon as the swap commits. Without the view, normalizing would mean rewriting every dashboard query on cutover day; with it, the rewrite becomes incremental. Repoint your hottest queries at the narrow table when it suits you. The rewrite happens on your schedule, not on cutover day's.

Dependent objects do not follow a rename. Continuous aggregates, retention and compression policies, triggers, and grants all stay bound to the renamed-away table. In our drill a real continuous aggregate kept aggregating sensor_readings_old, and nothing reported it: the rollup simply stopped seeing new rows the moment ingest moved to the narrow table. This is the class of failure most likely to cost you real data.

Inventory every dependent object before the swap, while the table still has its original name.

Then re-point each one after the swap. A continuous aggregate cannot be re-targeted, so recreate it against sensor_readings_narrow (joined to tag_metadata if it groups by a descriptor, which continuous aggregates support from TimescaleDB 2.10; note that only changes to the hypertable are tracked, so an edit to a metadata row does not reach the aggregate until you refresh it by hand), add its refresh policy back, and drop the old one once the new one has caught up. Triggers get recreated on the narrow table. Grants on the old table become grants on the view, since that is what the old readers now hit.

Treat retention policies as the dangerous ones, and re-create them last. A policy added to the narrow table judges every chunk you just moved on its first run, measured from now(), and any chunk older than drop_after goes immediately. In our drill a re-created 365-day policy over history whose newest rows were already older than a year deleted every chunk within seconds. Before you add the policy back, compare its window against the oldest chunk the narrow table now holds, and decide on purpose whether that history is meant to survive. If it is, the policy waits until you have moved or archived it. The old table's own retention policy is the mirror problem: it followed sensor_readings_old into retirement and keeps dropping chunks from the fallback you are counting on. Pause it with the same alter_job call right after the swap.

Keep the old table until old and new agree on the overlap. Ingest is writing to the narrow table, the view is serving reads from it, and sensor_readings_old is still there untouched. Hold that reconciliation window open until the checks below pass.

The cheap check is per-slice row counts, using the counts the control table already recorded.

An empty result means every slice moved as many rows as the wide table held for that window. A row means either the inner join dropped a tag in that slice or ingest was still landing in that window when the slice ran; the failure table below has the move.

The stronger check is a per-day checksum over a sample window on both sides: row count and first and last timestamp compared exactly, and the sum of every value compared with a relative tolerance. The tolerance is doing real work. Two full scans sum a hundred million doubles in a different physical order, and an exact comparison of the sums fails on floating-point rounding with no row out of place. In our validation run a seven-day checksum came back with zero mismatches.

Only when both checks pass, and your dashboards have run a normal cycle against the view, drop sensor_readings_old. That is also the moment to re-enable the columnstore job you paused in the schema step, with the same alter_job call and scheduled => true. Until you drop the old table, the cutover is a reversible rename.

If a step fails before then, find your row.

Step 1 trips the UNIQUE constraint on tag_name

You are in the lifecycle case from Step 0. Stop and re-scope; do not weaken the constraint.

Crash, kill, or timeout inside the transaction

Re-run the slice. The transaction rolled back whole and the primary key on slice_start makes a blind retry safe.

A tag was registered after the backfill and the inner join dropped it, or ingest was still landing in the window when the slice ran

Re-run Step 1, delete that slice's rows and its control row, and run the slice again from sensor_readings_old.

The loop was driven from a high-water mark

Ask migration_slices which windows are missing and run those.

pg_index WHERE indisvalid IS FALSE finds it. Drop it and rebuild.

Retry during a quiet minute. Do not remove the lock_timeout.

The view does not expose a column that query selects

An aggregate or policy still reads the old table

A narrow hypertable, a metadata table with one row per tag, dashboards that never noticed the swap, and an old table you can still fall back to until you choose not to. Before you book the window, rehearse it. Run Step 0 tonight. Then copy one week of your wide table into a scratch schema, run Steps 1 through 4 against it with the same freeze in place, and kill a slice mid-run on purpose so you see the rollback happen on your own hardware. And if you would rather not own the columnstore and retention policies you just re-created by hand, Tiger Cloud manages the hypertable, compression, and policies. If the rehearsal leaves you wanting a second pair of eyes before the real window, TigerData's support plans put PostgreSQL and TimescaleDB experts on the other end of the ticket.

The float-only schema keeps every step above readable, and plenty of telemetry tables really are all measurements. When yours also carry pump run states, valve positions, alarm codes, or a text mode label, the standard fix is what TigerData calls the medium table layout: one nullable value column per data type instead of one value column for everything. A new tag still costs one metadata row; only a new data type costs a column.

The float column keeps the name value, so the Step 4 view still serves the old value column unchanged for every measurement tag. The CHECK enforces exactly one value per row and needs no lookup, so unlike a foreign key it stays cheap on the ingest path. The rest of the migration changes in three places:

RAG Complexity Is a Bet Against the Model

#9865. Welcome FLUX.3 Image Klein in Diffusers

Black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one. One model does text-to-image and multi-reference image-to-image, and it adds something new, the layout control. You write bounding boxes into the prompt to say where each part of the image should go, or which parts of a reference image to move.

Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection:

You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!

Install the latest diffusers and transformers (for the Qwen3-VL text encoder):

Load the distilled checkpoint and generate an image:

FLUX.3 responds best to a full scene description with the subject, the setting, the light, the composition, and the style. The official prompting guide from Black Forest Labs has more tips. The distilled checkpoint generates a 1024 × 1024 image in 16 steps by default. Pass height, width, or num_inference_steps to change them.

Pass a reference image (or more) with the image argument. Write the prompt as a caption of the image you want, with the change included.

With several references, refer to them in the prompt as , , ... in the order they are passed to image:

Add a JSON list of regions after the caption. Each region has an id, a bbox, and a desc, and the caption mentions it as .

Boxes are written as [y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max], y first, on a 0–1000 scale. Because the scale is normalized, the same box works at any image size.

For edits, each region says where its content comes from (src_bbox in the reference) and where it goes (tgt_bbox in the output). A region with the same two boxes stays where it is.

This example moves the knitted knight up and to the left, and pins the backdrop, the cliff, the needle, the dragon, and the fire:

Everything above uses the distilled checkpoint. The base checkpoint runs 50 steps with classifier-free guidance, and it's the one to fine-tune (see LoRA finetuning).

Black Forest Labs also ships the transformer as a single file, in bf16 and in two quantized formats: fp8r (rowwise FP8) and nvfp4. Load any of them with from_single_file, then load the other components by name so the bf16 transformer isn't downloaded too.

For the unquantized single file, use https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/model.safetensors and drop quantization_config.

FLUX.3 works for both text-to-image and image-to-image, which makes it a great base for custom LoRAs. diffusers ships DreamBooth LoRA training scripts for both tasks (you can also train with Ostris' AI Toolkit).

Here is a text-to-image example that learns a tarot-card style from the multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain dataset, triggered with trtcrd:

To reduce memory usage, add a few optimization flags:

--gradient_checkpointing recomputes activations in the backward pass (lower VRAM, slightly slower), --cache_latents pre-encodes the images and frees the VAE, and --use_8bit_adam keeps the optimizer states in 8-bit.

A couple of knobs are worth experimenting with. The grid below trains the same tarot style with different LoRA ranks and optimizers; the adapters are on the Hub at diffusers-modular/flux3-tarot-lora. More training features and configurations are documented in the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README.

For instruction-based editing, the image-to-image script (train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein_img2img.py) trains on (reference image, target image, instruction) triplets, where the reference is addressed in the prompt as .

See the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README for all options and the full image-to-image example.

In this section, we will talk about the memory consumption and the speed of generation of the models.

End-to-end timings for the distilled checkpoint (16 steps), averaged over three runs after a warmup:

Single NVIDIA H100 80GB, no offloading, default attention backend.

A reference image roughly doubles the time. Reference tokens join the same sequence as the text and the image being generated, so a 1024 × 1024 reference adds 4,096 tokens to every transformer call

Let's open the model up, one piece at a time. The model takes three kinds of tokens:

FLUX.3 is a latent-space flow model for image generation. This means that the denoiser takes latents as inputs and produces latents as outputs. We use a VAE to decode the latents back to pixels. FLUX.3 uses the same VAE architecture as Flux.2.

The FLUX.2 VAE compresses an image 8× in each direction into 32 channels, and then every 2 × 2 patch of that latent is packed into a single token with 128 channels.

So one token covers a 16 × 16 pixel patch, and a 1024 × 1024 image becomes a 64 × 64 grid of 4,096 tokens. The noisy image starts as random noise of exactly that shape. A reference image goes through the same VAE encoder and packing, and keeps its own size.

The text encoder is Qwen3-VL, a vision-language model. FLUX.3 doesn't just take its last layer. It reads the hidden states of eight of its 36 layers (layers 4, 8, …, 32) and stacks them, so each text token becomes a 8 × 2560 = 20,480-dimensional vector before a linear layer projects it to the transformer's width of 3072.

This gives the transformer features from several depths of the language model, not just its final layer. The prompt is padded to a multiple of 80 tokens, and the transformer attends to the padding too, which is why the pipeline takes one prompt per call.

The transformer processes the tokens in two stages:

The two stages differ in who can attend to whom.

In stage 1, each stream only attends to itself, so each kind of token gets refined on its own terms first. In stage 2, everything attends to everything, where the image learns from the text and from the references. For comparison, FLUX.2's double-stream blocks also give text and image separate weights, but let them attend to each other from the start. FLUX.3 keeps the streams fully apart first, then merges them.

At the end, the text and reference tokens are simply dropped. Only the image tokens go through the output layers, which predict how to move them one step toward a clean image.

Every block, in either stage, has the same shape. Attention and the MLP run in parallel on the same normalized input, and their sum is added back to the residual stream.

Each block starts with a LayerNorm that has no learned scale or shift of its own. The scale, shift, and gate come from a timestep embedding instead (this is called modulation). Inside the attention, the queries and keys are RMS-normalized and get rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which we look at below.

In a joint block, all tokens share the same weights, but text, image, and reference tokens each get their own scale, shift, and gate.

In FLUX.1 and FLUX.2, one timestep embedding modulates every token. In FLUX.3, the modulation depends on the kind of token.

The noisy image tokens are modulated by the current timestep t. The text and reference tokens are always modulated by timestep 0, which means "clean, nothing to denoise here". So even a reference that looks almost the same as the output is marked as given context, not as something to generate.

The distilled checkpoint is a flow map. It is also told the timestep each step jumps to. That second timestep gets its own embedding, which is added to every token's modulation, so each of its 16 steps can make a larger jump.

Attention on its own doesn't know where a token is (this phenomenon is called permutation equivariance). RoPE fixes that by rotating each query and key by an amount that depends on the token's position. FLUX.3 uses four position axes, (t, h, w, l) (timestep, height, width, length of sequence), and gives each one a quarter (32 dimensions) of every 128-dimensional attention head:

Text tokens line up along l, like words in a sentence. The image and the references are 2D grids in (h, w), separated from each other along l. Because a reference uses the same (h, w) coordinates as the output, "the same spot in the reference" has a precise meaning to the model, which is what the src_bbox / tgt_bbox editing relies on.

FLUX.3 is a flow-matching model. Generation starts from pure noise, and at each of the 50 steps the transformer predicts a velocity. This is the direction from noise toward a clean image. The scheduler takes one step along it.

At every step you can also read off the model's current guess of the final image. Decoding that guess at a few steps shows how the image takes shape:

The fox, its pose, and the light are already in place by step 10, while the noise level is still 0.97. The snow-laden branches and the texture of the fur only appear in the last few steps. FLUX.3's scheduler uses a large time shift (6.93), which keeps the noise level high for most of the run: 44 of the 50 steps happen above σ = 0.5. We built this figure by adding one small block to the pipeline, which brings us to Modular Diffusers.

If you are new to flow matching, we have a beginner friendly tutorial and a video for you to understand how it works.

FLUX.3 ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline.

You can list the workflows and print the exact blocks of each one, without loading any weights.

get_workflow() resolves the auto branches and gives you the plain sequence of steps that will run. print(blocks.get_workflow("image_conditioned").doc) prints the components, inputs, defaults, and outputs of that workflow.

Pop the text encoder out, encode the prompt once, free it, and generate from the cached embeddings.

The denoising figure above came from one extra block that records the model's guess of the clean image at every step:

#9864. Microsoft's AI Risk Report Misses This Key Detail

The latest "Digital Defense Report" identifies government agencies as prime targets for AI attacks but doesn't mention that they are broadly being targeted through Microsoft bugs.

AI is changing cybersecurity. The hope is that software will eventually ship with fewer vulnerabilities, while the expectation in the meantime is that vendors will issue eye-popping volumes of software patches as a result of using AI to identify flaws in existing products. Software customers will increasingly use AI to more effectively and efficiently protect their networks. These promising developments will take time to unfold, as vendors and their customers learn how to incorporate AI into their software development and cybersecurity risk management workflows.

Attackers, meanwhile, are already using AI to generate novel attacks and orchestrate increasingly complex and large-scale hacking campaigns. AI is already enabling criminal groups to achieve hacking successes normally reserved for patient, highly resourced nation-state threat actors. And nation-state threat actors are using AI to increase the scale and sophistication of their cyber operations. The threat level is rising at an alarming rate.

Related:Philippine Migrant Worker Data Likely Leaked in 69GB Government Breach

Microsoft flagged the impacts of AI on cybersecurity in its recently released "2026 Digital Defense Report." Among its findings, it assessed that government agencies and services were the most affected by cyber threats and frequently targeted for nation-state activity.

Microsoft's report has a major blind spot, however: the impact of legacy software, especially its own, on organizations' cyber-risk. Legacy software will remain the substrate of organizations' attack surface for the foreseeable future. Vendors need to up their security game, and their customers need to demand better security from their vendors, particularly as AI heightens the threat landscape.

For example, with an 85% market share, Microsoft is the most dominant player in the US public sector productivity software market. Its products are therefore a prime target for state-sponsored groups seeking access to US government agencies and the data and secrets they are charged with protecting. So we should expect attackers to prize vulnerabilities in Microsoft's products and devote a substantial proportion of their hacking efforts to these popular products.

But there is more to the story than Microsoft's sheer prevalence in federal IT. Microsoft's grip on the federal IT market exposes the US government to a disproportionate share of cyber vulnerabilities. According to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Microsoft accounts for nearly 16% of known exploited vulnerabilities (KEVs) so far this year — the most of any company. Microsoft accounts for nearly 23% of known exploited vulnerabilities from November 2021 (when CISA began tracking KEVs) to October 2026.

Related:One Compromised Laptop, Billions Lost: The Binance Attack-Path Warning

By comparison, the next-highest vendor, Cisco, is responsible for approximately 7% in 2026 and 6% total, less than half of Microsoft's share.

Some agencies even rely on Microsoft as their single software vendor. This isn't particularly surprising — Microsoft has a track record of locking customers into its ecosystem by bundling its cloud computing offerings with office and security products (bundling is one area of focus of the Federal Trade Commission’s ongoing antitrust investigation into Microsoft) and then making it too difficult or costly for customers to switch vendors.

In 2023, the US Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) discontinued its Data Loss Prevention program after moving to bundle security tools into a sole-source Microsoft enterprise license. The move reportedly put 18 million veterans' personal records at risk of leakage. The VA has now moved to reverse course by seeking alternatives to Microsoft, having recognized the consequences of a Microsoft monoculture. Lesson learned.

Related:PapRAT Cyber-Espionage Campaign Leaves a 'Bitter' Taste in South Asia

Microsoft's Digital Defense Report identifies how frequently government agencies are affected by cyber threats and targeted for nation-state activity. Microsoft knows this firsthand. Since 2023, Chinese state-sponsored actors have compromised Microsoft products in at least two significant instances, accessing over two dozen US government agencies' emails in one attack and compromising at least seven agencies in another in July 2025.

Russian state-backed actors have also exploited Microsoft's weak security at least three times since 2020, including the infamous SolarWinds attack and an operation to exfiltrate emails between Microsoft personnel and government agencies. US government officials and advisory bodies have concluded that these breaches were preventable and caused by Microsoft's negligence. The reach and severity of breaches will only grow as China, Russia, and other nation-state threat actors become AI-native and AI tools become increasingly sophisticated.

Microsoft deserves some credit for using AI to evaluate products it has already deployed: its record-setting Patch Tuesday count of 974 vulnerabilities disclosed last month is no doubt the result of using AI to identify flaws. But that's not good enough.

All software vendors, including Microsoft, should invest more in the security of their products before they are released, even if it comes at the expense of slowing the rollout of new product features. And they should all be transparent to customers about these processes to enable customers to make more informed purchasing decisions. Otherwise, Microsoft's "2027 Digital Defense Report" will paint an even darker picture of the threat environment.

Director of the Program on Geopolitics, Technology, and Governance, Stanford University

Andrew Grotto founded and directs the Program on Geopolitics, Technology, and Governance at Stanford University's Center for International Security and Cooperation. He serves as the faculty lead for the Cyber Policy and Security specialization in Stanford’s master’s in international policy program, where he teaches courses on cyber policy and economic statecraft. He is also a visiting fellow at the Hoover Institution. Previously, he was senior advisor to the Secretary of Commerce for technology policy during the Obama administration and Senior Director for Cyber Policy on the National Security Council in the Obama and Trump administrations. He advises technology companies on digital risks, including companies that compete with Microsoft.

#9863. Welcome Muse Spark Open: open-weight frontier multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta

Muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta. The mixture of experts model brings text, images, audio, and video into a model with approximately 816 billion parameters, around 42 billion active per token, and a context window of up to one million tokens. It generates text, giving developers a common interface for asking questions about different kinds of input.

Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.

Meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools. It also takes images, audio, and video as input, so the same model can read a screenshot, listen to a voice note, or watch a screen recording while it works on your code. This post shows you how to run it, how to fine-tune it, and what we built with it. Find all the models here.

Meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained on real developer workflows such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions. Muse Spark Open is an agentic focused model that plans, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long tasks, including browsing the web with images.

The checkpoint repositories are Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B and Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4.

Muse Spark Open is the full-size model of the Muse series of models. Muse Glimmer, which Meta released in August, is a small dense model from the same series, ideal for running locally. Both models use the same tokenizer and vocabulary. The chat template follows the Muse Glimmer template, with additions for the new modalities. In Muse Spark Open the input embedding and the output layer are separate matrices of about 1.66B parameters each.

The language model has 62 layers and a hidden dimension of 8192. Each layer has 128 query heads and 16 key-value heads (grouped-query attention). Each head has 64 dimensions. The attention block has an output gate and an output normalization layer. The model also applies normalization to the queries and the keys (QK-norm). Each block combines its input and its output through a learned residual gate, not through a plain sum.

Muse Glimmer uses one dense feed-forward network in each layer. Muse Spark Open replaces this dense network with a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) block. Each MoE block has 256 experts, and a router selects 8 experts for each token. Each expert is a feed-forward network that projects from 8192 to 4096 dimensions and back to 8192, then applies its own normalization to its output. The experts hold ~97% of the total model parameters.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 42B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of an 816B-parameter model, but runs at the much faster speed of a 42B model. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1.5 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores the parameters in 4-bit precision with negligible loss in accuracy, specifically for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. In transformers, the BF16 checkpoint runs across 4 nodes of 8 H200 GPUs with tensor parallelism (TP=32) and the NVFP4 runs on a single B200 node. If you want to deploy Muse Spark Open, check out the llama.cpp, vLLM, and SGLang recipes below.

A perception encoder converts images and video frames into tokens for the language model, just like Muse Glimmer. The encoder has 1.8B parameters, 50 layers, a hidden dimension of 1536, and 16 attention heads. It splits each image into 14×14 patches and produces features with 4096 dimensions. Position information comes from learned absolute embeddings and 2D RoPE. The feed-forward network in each layer uses LayerNorm and GELU. Every fourth layer and the last layer use full attention, and the other layers use sparse attention.

Muse Glimmer 30B uses an encoder with the same architecture. The design follows the Perception Encoder work from Meta. Video input goes through the same encoder as images.

Muse Spark Open accepts audio as input through its audio encoder. An audio tokenizer converts the audio into tokens, and the chat template marks the audio position with <|audio|> tokens. The encoder emits one audio token every 80 ms, which yields 12.5 tokens per second. So let’s say, you have an audio of 10 seconds, the number of input audio tokens would be 125. The encoder itself is a convolutional pyramid where each stage consists of a patch embedder of different patch sizes and 2 convolutional blocks of 1d kernels of size 7 with stride of 1. These stages are repeated for patch sizes of [16, 6, 5, 4]. At the end of the final stage, the temporal frames are fed to a final block of RMSNorm → linear projection → RMSNorm.

The context window is 1M tokens at inference. The configuration sets max_position_embeddings to 1,048,576. This includes image, video, and audio tokens in the same window as text.

Grouped-query attention keeps the KV cache small for a model of this size. Each token adds 2 × 16 heads × 64 dimensions × 62 layers = 126,976 values to the cache. In BF16, this is about 250 KB per token and about 266 GB for a full 1M-token context.

The Muse Spark Open implementation provides MuseSparkForConditionalGeneration for text generation from multimodal inputs and MuseSparkProcessor for preparing conversations. The processor combines the tokenizer, image and video processors, audio feature extractor, and chat template.

Use a DistributedConfig to configure the parallelism settings. tp_size is the number of devices across which the dense layers are sharded, and ep_size is the number of devices across which the experts are distributed.

You can initialize the model and processor as follows.

Prepare the conversation, then pass the messages to processor.apply_chat_template, enabling add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=True, return_dict=True, and return_tensors="pt". Pass the processor output to model.generate and decode the newly generated tokens, excluding the input prefix. The processor has a lever for the reasoning effort, mapping symbolic levels (low/medium/high/xhigh) to the integers the model itself accepts (16, 64, 256, 512). Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task. You can also set a numeric effort by including a line like Reasoning strength: 1 in the system prompt.

The Muse Spark Open processor expands each image marker into the number of patch tokens required by the processed image, surrounded by image boundary tokens. This expansion keeps the text positions aligned with the visual features passed to the model. The processor also handles multiple images within a single prompt.

Video prompts include frame timing as well as visual content. The processor handles videos with audios in them (which is an upgrade from Muse Glimmer thanks to the audio encoder). The processor downsamples video frames and audio to align frames together. By default, videos are sampled to 2 FPS, capped at 96 frames. You can modify this by setting the fps of the video processor:

As a general rule of thumb, videos are frames in temporal sequence, and the more you downsample, the more you will lose frames in between specific events, so you need to keep fps high if you want more accurate generations. However, there’s a trade-off because you will require more memory and increase latency for prefill. The frames are interleaved with text input that states timestamps (e.g. “Time: 3.5s”). To enable passing in videos with audio, pass load_audio_from_video=True to apply_chat_template.

Preserve the video's metadata when preparing inputs with return_metadata=True so the processor can assign the correct framerate.

The Muse Spark Open audio tower consumes a raw waveform. The processor expects mono audio at 24 kHz and pads the waveform to a multiple of 1,920 samples, corresponding to one audio embedding per 80 milliseconds. Audio supplied directly to the processor at another sample rate must first be resampled. You can do this by using the load_audio util of transformers. load_audio uses torchcodec, librosa or torchaudio backends, so make sure to have one of these installed locally before running inference.

If you want to simply use apply_chat_template with messages though, this is all handled for you under the hood:

The processor inserts the matching number of audio tokens between audio boundary markers. It also returns a mask identifying real samples, allowing the model to exclude padded audio embeddings.

Muse Spark Open can do text-only and multimodal tool calling. You can make the model call tools as follows.

Muse Spark Open uses a channel-based chat template (Harmony, first introduced by gpt-oss). Note that you don’t have to know about the internals, but it’s useful to check the channels the model routes to, in case you get low quality outputs. In the input message below:

<|start|>assistant is intentionally left open, it’s the model that chooses recipient with to= . The model has different recipients, e.g. self asks the model to reason,

self is for reasoning, commentary are comments before and between tool calls visible to the end user, user is the final response.Tool-call routing is parsed as follows (assuming you have passed tools to apply_chat_template:

Muse Spark Open is integrated in llama.cpp and comes in the prebuilt binaries. You can install this with following command:

You can start the server as follows with quant suffix attached to model ID:

The repository containing quants is here. Once the server has started, you can head to localhost:9931 to chat with the built-in WebUI. From the web UI you can add audio and images for inference and adjust the reasoning lever.Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task.We tested quants on Mac M3 Ultra (512GB). An imatrix-calibrated 2-bit quant runs at 18 tokens/s, with plenty of room free for the KV cache (304 GB used by the model).

You can also query the server as follows. Feel free to check out the API reference for multimodality, tool calls and more.

llama.cpp team ships different quantized versions. We have tested Q2_K, Q4_K_S and Q_8 on Apple Silicon chips. You can run each quant by adding the quant id as suffix, llama serve -hf ggml-org/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B:Q2_K.

The Muse Spark Open integration for SGLang supports text, image, audio, and video inputs. The NVFP4 reference configuration runs across four GB300 GPUs.

From the SGLang integration environment, download the checkpoint from the Hugging Face Hub and start the server:

The checkpoint includes the chat template, which we pass explicitly. The launcher configures the Muse reasoning and tool-call parsers.

Send a request through the OpenAI-compatible API:

The response separates the reasoning trace in reasoning_content from the final answer in content.

The Muse Spark Open reference integration for vLLM supports text and image inputs with the NVFP4 checkpoint that require blackwell series GPUs.

After installing the reference plugin and its dependencies, download the checkpoint from the Hugging Face Hub and launch the server:

This configuration sets a 128K-token serving context. The plugin supplies the model implementation, checkpoint loader, and reasoning and tool-call parsers.

Send a request using the same Hub model ID:

Muse Spark Open is available in oMLX and mlx-lm today. oQ quants optimized for oMLX are available in 3-bit and 4-bit, ready to use right away.

We tested the oQ3e quant on an M3 Ultra (512 GB). The model takes about 344 GB, leaving room for the KV cache, and runs at about 225 tok/s prefill and 21 tok/s generation with a 1024-token prompt and 128 generated tokens.

Once you download the model through the oMLX interface, you can chat with it in the built-in chat UI. From the chat UI you can add images and adjust the reasoning effort on the fly, from low to xhigh. The model’s reasoning shows up as a collapsible thinking block, separate from the final answer.

Note that it's not possible to turn reasoning off, and the default (Auto) uses xhigh. Set it to “low” if you want to use fewer tokens on easier tasks.

The language model is also available in this PR of the official mlx-lm repository. You can run it on the same high-quality oQ3e quant like this:

This is a big model, even the 3-bit quantization requires more than 256 GB of RAM, as explained above. You can also run distributed inference across multiple computers, please refer to the documentation for details.

You can deploy Muse Spark Open on Inference Endpoints with a pre-validated SGLang recipe for the NVFP4 variant which runs on either 8 × NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 98 GB with 131072 context length, or with 8 x NVIDIA H200 141GB if you want 1048576 context length instead.

To deploy, run one command with the Hugging Face CLI:

Or open endpoints.huggingface.co/new/meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 and select Create Endpoint.

The endpoint exposes an OpenAI-compatible API with both Chat Completions API at /v1/chat/completions and Responses API at /v1/responses.

Any OpenAI-compatible client works with the same URL and your Hugging Face token as the API key.

You can fine-tune the 816B checkpoint with the TRL SFTTrainer. This section shows how we fine-tuned it with TRL on 8 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. The recipe trains LoRA adapters on the attention layers. The experts stay frozen. The full script is in the TRL examples.

First, we need to split the model across 64 GPU devices. Given the large size of the model, we need to parallelize it across multiple axes. We shard the model with FSDP and split the experts across GPUs, using DistributedConfig, which tells transformers how to split the model when it loads:

In the snippet above, fsdp_size=64 shards the model across all 64 GPUs with FSDP2, and ep_size=8 splits the 256 experts of each layer into 8 groups. Transformers sends each token to the GPU that holds its expert, so each GPU trains on its own slice of the batch.

Now, we can configure the SFTConfig for our training run. We’ve performed a simple task here to adapt the model’s chat template on an open source dataset, but you could apply it to your own use case.

The core parts here are packing=True which joins examples into 2048-token sequences without padding. A block-diagonal mask keeps the examples separate. save_only_model=True saves the adapter and no optimizer state, because the trainer cannot resume a model that was sharded at load time. LoraConfig targets the four attention projections and the 256 experts of each layer stay frozen.

Then we can run this command across each node:

We trained for 500 steps, which took about 2 hours on 64 H100s, at about 8,000 tokens per second. Mean token accuracy rose from 72% to 84% and the loss fell from 1.26 to 0.57, which signals a good fine-tuning run.

Muse Spark Open is a coding and agentic model. We wanted to see that for ourselves, so we tried a mixture of multi-modal and agentic tasks that use the model's image and audio inputs. Everything below is something you can run or fork.

We combined 2-bit quantized Muse Spark open (served on llama.cpp) with the Pi coding agent to generate and iteratively improve 3D assets in Three.js. You can find the prompt here, as the model is quantized it requires a bit more steering. We get 18 TPS on llama.cpp on Mac Ultra.

We initially describe the asset, and Pi uses the model to generate Three.js code for the asset, renders the result in a browser, and captures screenshots from multiple angles. It then sends those images back to the same model on llama server for visual feedback. Pi uses that feedback to edit the code and repeats the process.

We tested Spark on computer use tasks and were amazed by the performance, so we have built a lean demo that also serves to teach you how a computer use agent works. You can also further customize this for your needs. This is both an educational example and something you can run in a few lines. You can find it here.

Muse Spark NVFP4 Browser Agent with OpenEnv and HF Sandboxes

Hugging Face Sandboxes are sandboxes built on Hugging Face Jobs for easy code execution. The demo consists of three components:

where the remote sandbox contains the environment and the browser as illustrated below.

You can easily try this with a few steps, described in the example. Start Inference Endpoint with Muse Spark Open (NVFP4 works well too!), add your endpoint URL as environmental variable, publish your OpenEnv server in Spaces and also provide that, then you can run the agent loop. Muse Spark Open sees the previous actions, system prompt, url and the screenshot of the browser to take an action, and nothing else (no DOM, no HTML code, nothing) so it’s a truly multimodal browser demo.

Finally, we wanted to push Spark’s agentic multimodality to the limits, so we set up this space that combines the model’s audio, image, and agentic properties into a browser agent. We give the model a general description of a thing we need and it interacts with the integrated browser to find options on Amazon.

Muse Spark Open takes the voice input and reasons over the type of product that meets the descriptions, searches for it on Amazon, and selects the most appropriate based on criteria.

Muse Spark Open is a full-size open-weight model from the Muse series. Start with the BF16 or NVFP4 checkpoint, or try one of the great llama.cpp quants. If you build something with Muse Spark Open, share it, and tell us in the repository’s discussions.

#9862. Most Frequently Asked Questions About NFTs(Non-Fungible Tokens)

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) are the most popular digital assets today, capturing the attention of cryptocurrency investors, whales and people from around the world. People find it amazing that some users spend thousands or millions of dollars on a single NFT-based image of a monkey or other token, but you can simply take a screenshot for free. So here we share some freuently asked question about NFTs.

NFT stands for non-fungible  token, which is a cryptographic token on a blockchain with unique identification codes that distinguish it from other tokens. NFTs are unique and not interchangeable, which means no two NFTs are the same. NFTs can be a unique artwork, GIF, Images, videos, Audio album. in-game items, collectibles etc.

A blockchain is a distributed digital ledger that allows for the secure storage of data. By recording any kind of information—such as bank account transactions, the ownership of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs), or Decentralized Finance (DeFi) smart contracts—in one place, and distributing it to many different computers, blockchains ensure that data can’t be manipulated without everyone in the system being aware.

The value of an NFT comes from its ability to be traded freely and securely on the blockchain, which is not possible with other current digital ownership solutionsThe NFT points to its location on the blockchain, but doesn’t necessarily contain the digital property. For example, if you replace one bitcoin with another, you will still have the same thing. If you buy a non-fungible item, such as a movie ticket, it is impossible to replace it with any other movie ticket because each ticket is unique to a specific time and place.

One of the unique characteristics of non-fungible tokens (NFTs) is that they can be tokenised to create a digital certificate of ownership that can be bought, sold and traded on the blockchain.

As with crypto-currency, records of who owns what are stored on a ledger that is maintained by thousands of computers around the world. These records can’t be forged because the whole system operates on an open-source network.

NFTs also contain smart contracts—small computer programs that run on the blockchain—that give the artist, for example, a cut of any future sale of the token.

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) aren't cryptocurrencies, but they do use blockchain technology. Many NFTs are based on Ethereum, where the blockchain serves as a ledger for all the transactions related to said NFT and the properties it represents.5) How to make an NFT?

Anyone can create an NFT. All you need is a digital wallet, some ethereum tokens and a connection to an NFT marketplace where you’ll be able to upload and sell your creations

When you purchase a stock in NFT, that purchase is recorded on the blockchain—the bitcoin ledger of transactions—and that entry acts as your proof of ownership.

The value of an NFT varies a lot based on the digital asset up for grabs. People use NFTs to trade and sell digital art, so when creating an NFT, you should consider the popularity of your digital artwork along with historical statistics.

In the year 2021, a digital artist called Pak created an artwork called The Merge. It was sold on the Nifty Gateway NFT market for $91.8 million.

Non-fungible tokens can be used in investment opportunities. One can purchase an NFT and resell it at a profit. Certain NFT marketplaces let sellers of NFTs keep a percentage of the profits from sales of the assets they create.

Many people want to buy NFTs because it lets them support the arts and own something cool from their favorite musicians, brands, and celebrities. NFTs also give artists an opportunity to program in continual royalties if someone buys their work. Galleries see this as a way to reach new buyers interested in art.

There are many places to buy digital assets, like opensea and their policies vary. On top shot, for instance, you sign up for a waitlist that can be thousands of people long. When a digital asset goes on sale, you are occasionally chosen to purchase it.

To mint an NFT token, you must pay some amount of gas fee to process the transaction on the Etherum blockchain, but you can mint your NFT on a different blockchain called Polygon to avoid paying gas fees. This option is available on OpenSea and this simply denotes that your NFT will only be able to trade using Polygon's blockchain and not Etherum's blockchain. Mintable allows you to mint NFTs for free without paying any gas fees.

The answer is no. Non-Fungible Tokens are minted on the blockchain using cryptocurrencies such as Etherum, Solana, Polygon, and so on. Once a Non-Fungible Token is minted, the transaction is recorded on the blockchain and the contract or license is awarded to whoever has that Non-Fungible Token in their wallet.

You can sell your work and creations by attaching a license to it on the blockchain, where its ownership can be transferred. This lets you get exposure without losing full ownership of your work. Some of the most successful projects include Cryptopunks, Bored Ape Yatch Club NFTs, SandBox, World of Women and so on. These NFT projects have gained popularity globally and are owned by celebrities and other successful entrepreneurs. Owning one of these NFTs gives you an automatic ticket to exclusive business meetings and life-changing connections.

That’s a wrap. Hope you guys found this article enlightening. I just answer some question with my limited knowledge about NFTs.
